## Worked verification example

### Ticket-specific check

**Acceptance gap:** this source record has no explicit outcome checklist. Recover a concrete operation and expected result from its technical description/comments before claiming acceptance; do not manufacture a feature requirement from a process-review title.



**Illustrative scenario for this concern (not an observed reproduction):** A remote reviewer emits output, then stops. Another remains silent but supplies a trustworthy progress signal. Neither low local CPU nor silence alone identifies quota exhaustion. Preserve partial output, try compatible alternatives where policy permits, and record cancellation/terminal cause without orphaning the owned child.

Apply the scenario to the exact operation, code paths and acceptance criteria in the retained description. Record the input, actual result, expected result, source revision and a durable artifact. A failure must be tied to this outcome before reopening; a passing unrelated suite must not close it.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

**Bug:** rig installs skills to `skills_target` (default `~/.agents/skills`), but the Claude Code harness discovers Skill-tool skills from `~/.claude/skills/` (symlinks resolving to ~/.agents/skills). rig never creates those symlinks, so rig-installed universal skills (dead-code-investigation, shell-timeouts, promise-durable-action, naming, …) are NOT loaded/listed by the harness — only the ~11 that the tools' own install-skill happened to symlink.

**Impact:** any 'extract universal rules into agent-tools skills, slim AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md' work is UNSAFE while this is broken — the rule appears 'self-advertised via a skill' but the skill is never loaded → the rule is silently lost.

**Fix:** `rig apply` (skills section) must idempotently symlink each enabled skill into the harness's discovery dir, keyed by harness kind (claude-code → ~/.claude/skills). Don't clobber real non-symlink dirs there. `rig status` reports link drift. (Manual fix applied on this machine: 39 skills symlinked, harness now lists them live. **Acceptance gap:** this source record has no explicit outcome checklist. Recover a concrete operation and expected result from its technical description/comments before claiming acceptance; do not manufacture a feature requirement from a process-review title.



**Illustrative scenario for this concern (not an observed reproduction):** A CLI is invoked from outside its repository with a valid input, an invalid input and an unavailable optional backend. Successful output, nonzero failure, cancellation and cleanup are separately asserted. A mock backend passing does not establish that a live account, local model or audio device was exercised.

Apply the scenario to the exact operation, code paths and acceptance criteria in the retained description. Record the input, actual result, expected result, source revision and a durable artifact. A failure must be tied to this outcome before reopening; a passing unrelated suite must not close it.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## What's wrong

When rig provisions a skill into the natively-scanned skills dir (`~/.agents/skills/<name>/`) and that path already exists with differing content, `on_conflict: backup` (the default) moves the prior dir to a **sibling** backup: `~/.agents/skills/<name>.rig-bak-<timestamp>/`.

That backup dir is STILL under `~/.agents/skills/` and still contains a `SKILL.md`. opencode (>=1.16) auto-scans `~/.agents/skills` natively (see `riglib/harness_skills.py` `HARNESS_NATIVE_SKILLS`), so it loads the backup as a second skill and emits **duplicate-skill-name warnings**.

Root cause: `riglib/actions/fsutil.py` `copy_tree(on_conflict='backup')` derives the backup path from `backup_path(target)` — a same-parent sibling. For a SKILL that parent is a scanned dir.

## Acceptance criteria

- A conflicting skill install (`copy_skill` with `on_conflict=backup`) backs the prior skill up to a location **NOT under the scanned skills dir** (e.g. a sibling `<skills_target>/../.rig-backups/<name>.<timestamp>/`).
- The backup still contains the prior `SKILL.md` (data preserved, just relocated).
- Only the SKILL backup destination changes; unrelated backups (tmux, mcp.json, settings.json, ship-delegator, etc.) are untouched.
- A regression test asserts the backup is outside the scanned skills dir.
- Full rig suite green.

Follow-up to the just-merged skills-registry fix (#56).

**Acceptance gap:** this source record has no explicit outcome checklist. Recover a concrete operation and expected result from its technical description/comments before claiming acceptance; do not manufacture a feature requirement from a process-review title.



**Illustrative scenario for this concern (not an observed reproduction):** The operator disables a managed integration and runs reconciliation. Only owned artifacts are removed; manual files are preserved. The same declared state drives apply and status. A managed-file comment names the supported configuration command rather than merely saying do not edit.

Apply the scenario to the exact operation, code paths and acceptance criteria in the retained description. Record the input, actual result, expected result, source revision and a durable artifact. A failure must be tied to this outcome before reopening; a passing unrelated suite must not close it.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## Defect

The repo's committed `rig.yaml` (line 72) still declares the **removed** MCP slot:

```yaml
mcp:
  items:
    review:
      enabled: true
      command: "review --mcp"
```

But:
- `review --mcp` was dropped in the review subcommand refactor (agent-tools #32).
- The agent-tools MCP catalog has **no** `mcp/review/` item — its `mcp/README.md` explicitly states *"`review/` — NOT an MCP ... its MCP slot (and the dead `review --mcp` registration) was removed."*
- rig's own error system already classifies `mcp.review` as a **removed slot** (`riglib/errors.py` `_REMOVED_SLOTS[("mcp","review")]`).

So rig's shipped template contradicts both the canonical catalog and rig's own removed-slot registry.

## Evidence (reproducible on current main)

```
$ PYTHONPATH=. uv run ... python -m riglib status --config rig.yaml
error: removed mcp slot: review
  why: `mcp.items.review` (removed in agent-tools #32 ...); declared in .../rig.yaml
  fix: remove `mcp.items.review` from .../rig.yaml
$ echo $?
4
```

`rig status` against the repo's **own** committed config exits **4**. `docs/config-schema.md` (line ~282) documents the same dead `review --mcp` command, so the human reference is wrong too.

### Why smoke didn't catch it
`tests/smoke.sh` status-checks a *synthetic* clean sample that intentionally omits `mcp.review`; it never runs `rig status` against the repo's OWN `rig.yaml`. The dead slot lives only in the shipped template + docs.

## Fix (fix-or-remove → remove, per ROADMAP §9)

Implementing a real review MCP server is out of scope (and the catalog deliberately doesn't have one). So **remove** the dead slot:

1. Drop `mcp.items.review` from `rig.yaml` (keep the `mcp` block; it has no concrete catalog item, so ship it with empty `items`).
2. Replace the dead `review --mcp` example in `docs/config-schema.md` with the catalog-endorsed code-search (serena) example.

## Acceptance criteria

- `rig status --config rig.yaml` (the repo's own committed config) exits **0** — no "removed mcp slot: review".
- No `review --mcp` string remains in `rig.yaml` or `docs/config-schema.md`.
- A **regression test** asserts the repo's own `rig.yaml` has no removed/unknown MCP slot (RED before the template fix, green after).
- Full pytest suite + `bash tests/smoke.sh` green; ruff clean.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

Part of the error-system v2 missing-target heuristic (PR #27).

## What

`rig status` / `rig doctor` resolve the harness settings file to scan for dead hook references via `_scan_missing_targets()` in `riglib/cli.py`, which is **hardcoded** to `~/.claude/settings.json`:

```python
settings = Path(_os.path.expanduser("~/.claude/settings.json"))
return scan_settings_hooks(settings)
```

Its own docstring flags this as unfinished: *"a future multi-harness expansion has one place to add settings paths."*

## Why this is a bug

rig now resolves the harness settings file per config — the `apply_harness`, `provision_permissions`, and `register_hook_bridge` plan actions all carry the resolved settings path as `action.target` (respecting a `permissions.settings_path` / `harness.settings_path` override and the harness kind, e.g. `auto` mode writes `~/.claude/settings.json` but the default project mode writes `.claude/settings.json` in the repo).

When a repo`s rig.yaml points the harness settings at a non-default path (a supported, validated config), the missing-target scan looks at the WRONG file (`~/.claude/settings.json`) and silently reports NOTHING — a dead hook in the actually-managed settings file goes unflagged. That is exactly the silent-success failure the error-system v2 was built to kill: a dead reference that surfaces only at runtime as a generic "PreToolUse error".

## How to fix

In `cmd_status` (which already has the loaded plan in scope), derive the settings file path(s) to scan from the planned `apply_harness` / `provision_permissions` / `register_hook_bridge` action targets (via `harness_settings_file`), deduped. Keep the `~/.claude/settings.json` fallback for `cmd_doctor` (no config loaded there). Scan every resolved path, not just the hardcoded default.

## Acceptance

- RED-first regression test: a plan whose harness settings target is a non-default path with a dead hook command → the missing-target scan finds it (hardcoded scan would miss it).
- `~/.claude/settings.json` fallback preserved for `rig doctor`.
- Full rig suite green; ruff clean.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## The gap

`rig apply` provisions universal skills, agent-hooks, the git-hooks dispatcher, harness mode, tmux, and the model-freshness cron — but it does **not** provision the personal CLI tool ecosystem (`tg`, `review`, `task`, `draw`, …). Those are each self-installed out of band via each tool's own `install.sh` + symlink into PATH + `<tool> install-skill`.

The CTO's correction (verbatim, tg#4579): *"Все надо через rig, в первую очередь нужен именно для установки экосистемы наших тулов tg, review и тд!"* — Everything must go through rig; rig is needed FIRST AND FOREMOST precisely for installing the ECOSYSTEM of our tools (tg, review, task, draw, …).

This is rig's PRIMARY purpose, and it's currently missing.

## The ask

Add a new machine-level provisioning category `tools:` so `rig apply` installs/updates and advertises the whole tool ecosystem, declaratively.

### Config shape (GLOBAL layer, `~/.config/rig/config.yaml`)

```yaml
tools:
  enabled: true          # opt-in (default OFF — absent block provisions nothing)
  items:
    tg:
      repo: ~/.files/repos/tg-cli
    review:
      repo: ~/xp/review-cli
    task:
      repo: ~/xp/task-cli
    draw:
      repo: ~/xp/draw-cli
```

Each tool is one config line + a repo path. `install` method runs the tool's OWN `install.sh` (locate repo → optional build → symlink bin into the managed PATH dir → `<tool> install-skill` to advertise). More tools = one more entry.

### Apply behavior

For each declared+enabled tool: ensure it's installed (run its `install.sh` when not already current), on PATH (symlink resolves), and advertised (`install-skill` → SessionStart blurb). **Idempotent** (re-apply is a no-op when current), **safe** (detect an existing working symlink to the same target — don't clobber), respects each tool's own install mechanism. Reports what it changed.

### Status / drift

`rig status` reports tool-install drift: a declared tool whose bin doesn't resolve (missing) or whose skill isn't advertised.

- [ ] `rig apply` installs a declared tool (symlink bin + run `install-skill`)
- [ ] idempotent re-apply is a no-op when already current

- [ ] `rig status` reports tool-install drift
- [ ] full rig suite green, ruff clean
- [ ] `rig apply` on the real machine: `which task tg review draw` all resolve, each advertised

PR #67 (836aefd, \"feat(provision): rig installs the personal CLI ecosystem\") added a new reconcile category \`\"tools\"\` — the personal CLI ecosystem (tg/review/task/draw). It correctly wired the plan action (\`_build_tools\` → \`provision_tools\`), config validation (\`config.py: _validate_tools\`), schema, the drift check (\`drift.py: _check_tools\`, emitting \`DriftItem(..., \"tools\", ...)\`), and the apply runner.

BUT it omitted \`\"tools\"\` from the TWO status-summary registries:

1. **\`riglib/areas.py\` — the \`AREAS\` tuple.** Its own module docstring calls it \"the SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH for the area list\" and warns: an area present in the plan but absent here is silently uncounted. There is no \`Area\` for \`\"tools\"\`, so \`rig status\` never prints a CLI-ecosystem line in the \"areas rig manages:\" summary — the ecosystem rig now manages is INVISIBLE in status (other GLOBAL areas like \"tg-ctl inbound daemon\" and \"tmux config\" do show a line; tools shows nothing).

2. **\`riglib/layers.py\` — the \`_CATEGORY_LAYER\` dict.** \`\"tools\"\` is absent; it falls through to the \`.get(category, GLOBAL)\` default. The default happens to be correct (tools IS a machine-wide GLOBAL concern), so no crash — but every other category is mapped EXPLICITLY, and the exhaustiveness guard test keys off this dict.

## Why the existing guard missed it

\`tests/test_status_areas.py::test_every_known_category_is_covered_by_some_area\` asserts \`set(_CATEGORY_LAYER) - {cats covered by AREAS}\` is empty. Because #67 added \`\"tools\"\` to NEITHER \`_CATEGORY_LAYER\` NOR \`AREAS\`, the category escaped both registries and the guard had nothing to compare — a coverage blind spot. The guard only catches a category that's in \`_CATEGORY_LAYER\` but missing an Area; it cannot catch a category that's in the plan/drift code but missing from both registries.

## User-facing consequence

A user who has opted into the personal CLI ecosystem (\`tools:\` block) cannot see it in \`rig status\` — the area heading never prints, so \"what does rig manage here, and where am I out of sync\" silently omits the ecosystem. Contradicts areas.py's own exhaustiveness contract.

## Fix (3 parts)

1. \`riglib/layers.py\`: add \`\"tools\": GLOBAL,\` to \`_CATEGORY_LAYER\`.
2. \`riglib/areas.py\`: add \`Area(\"tools\", \"personal CLI ecosystem (tg/review/task/draw/…)\", GLOBAL, (\"tools\",))\` to \`AREAS\` after \`tg_ctl\`.
3. TDD: strengthen the guard so a category in NEITHER registry is caught (introspect the categories \`drift.py\` actually emits + a targeted \`tools\` pin), plus a rendering test proving the ecosystem line shows under GLOBAL as drift.

## Acceptance criteria

- \`rig status\` prints a \"personal CLI ecosystem …\" line under the GLOBAL section when a \`tools:\` block is configured.
- \`_CATEGORY_LAYER\` and \`AREAS\` both cover \`\"tools\"\` explicitly.
- A guard test fails RED if any future plan/drift category is registered in neither registry.

## Existing related work

[agent-tools#92](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/92). These are observed references, not automatically asserted blocking dependencies.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## The gap

The `test_real_catalog_*` test family (and the require-ticket-provisioning test shipped as #72 / agent-tools#92, `test_real_catalog_provisions_require_ticket_guard`) **never runs in CI** — so those regression guards are theater. A regression would pass CI.

### Why (found by the #72 agent)

These tests `pytest.skip` when no agent-tools catalog is reachable (`Catalog.scan(None)` / `_agent_tools_source()` raises), and the two smoke-e2e legs are additionally `@pytest.mark.skipif(RIG_SMOKE_FAST_E2E != "1")`. Two CI jobs exist:

- **`test`** (unit suite) runs `python -m pytest -q` but has **NO catalog checked out** → every `test_real_catalog_*` SKIPS.
- **`real-catalog-smoke`** DOES fetch the catalog (sets `RIG_AGENT_TOOLS_SOURCE`) but runs `smoke.sh --fast`, and `--fast` **SKIPS the pytest leg entirely** (`smoke.sh` exits before its pytest section under `--fast`).

Net: the real-catalog pytest guards run ONLY under a full local `smoke.sh`, never in CI. So a regression — rig stops provisioning `require-ticket-before-commit`, or the `agent_hooks` default flips to opt-in, or a catalog rename rig can't resolve — is unit-GREEN and ships unguarded.

The three affected tests:
- `tests/test_errors.py::test_repo_rig_yaml_plans_clean_against_the_real_catalog`
- `tests/test_errors.py::test_real_catalog_provisions_require_ticket_guard`
- `tests/test_smoke_precommit.py::test_real_catalog_full_coverage_plans_every_item`

## The fix

Add a dedicated step to the existing `real-catalog-smoke` job (it already fetches the catalog and computes `$SRC`) that runs just the real-catalog pytest leg with both gates lifted: `RIG_AGENT_TOOLS_SOURCE=$SRC` (resolves the catalog so the `Catalog.scan` skips don't fire) AND `RIG_SMOKE_FAST_E2E=1` (lifts the opt-in `skipif`), selecting `-k real_catalog`. Includes a vacuous-pass guard: the step FAILS if the selector collected zero tests (a rename broke `-k`) or if any selected test SKIPPED (env-wiring broke and the gate would be theater again).

Prefer the targeted step over dropping `--fast`: `--fast` also gates off the heavy `rig init --yes` apply / skill-install / tg-ctl / harness-symlink legs (covered already by `cleanroom-e2e`); running the full smoke would add minutes of redundant, partly-flaky work just to reach the pytest leg.

## Acceptance

- The `real-catalog-smoke` job runs the three real-catalog pytest tests with a count > 0, none skipped, in the merge CI.
- A regression that un-provisions require-ticket (or flips the agent_hooks default to opt-in) now fails CI.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## CTO complaint (verbatim)
> Много текста а что сделано не ясно. И не ясно что и почему не сделано и не понятно почему нельзя управлять процессом и зачем вообще что-то делать если от пользователя не получено никаких указаний.

Context: `rig init` with no args, when the textual TUI isn't installed, fell back to a "non-interactive default setup" that SILENTLY wrote `rig.yaml` AND ran the full plan (mutating HOME) — with zero user consent, and output that read as if it had "done a bunch of things" when the plan is really a preview of what `rig apply` does.

## Redesign (three principles)
1. **No presumptuous side-effects** — a bare `rig init` with no way to run the wizard (no TTY, or `textual` absent) writes nothing, applies nothing; it prints a non-destructive PREVIEW + how to proceed.
2. **Clarity** — done vs preview vs skipped is unambiguous: `rig init --yes` writes `rig.yaml` ("config only; NOTHING applied yet"), the plan is labeled "PREVIEW of `rig apply`", an apply shows results (never a preview label).
3. **Control** — TUI wizard (Export vs Apply) stays the interactive surface; new `--apply` flag is the explicit one-shot; `rig apply` is the separate apply step.

## Breaking change (flagged for CTO veto)
`rig init --yes` now SCAFFOLDS ONLY (exit 0, nothing applied); the one-shot becomes `rig init --yes --apply`. All in-repo consumers updated.

### Ticket-specific check

**Operation under review:** gh ship broken machine-wide: rig apply pins AGENT_TOOLS_ROOT at a transient temp checkout.

**Original problem context (historical statement, not a new observation):** `rig apply` writes the machine-level `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/agent-tools/env` (AGENT_TOOLS_ROOT) that every repo's `gh ship` delegator sources when the env var is unset. The root was derived from `agent_tools_source`/`catalog.source` with no guard, so a one-off apply whose source resolved under a temp dir (a mkdtemp clone / $TMPDIR / /tmp — e.g. an agent testing agent-tools from a throwaway worktree) clobbered the durable pointer with a path that vanishes on cleanup. Observed 2026-07-09 on the CTO's machine: ``` AGENT_TOOLS_ROOT=/private/var/folders/1c/.../T/tmpdhx8hi2a/agent-tools ``` Once the tempdir is gone, `gh ship` exits 127 for EVERY repo on the machine (delegator sources a dead path) until someone manually re-points it. Every merger agent had to override `AGENT_TOOLS_ROOT=/Users/ultra/xp/agent-tools` to ship.

**Expected outcomes from this ticket, not invented from its title:**
- `rig apply` from a transient (temp-dir) agent-tools source never overwrites a persistent machine pointer with a temp path.
- An already-poisoned pointer (its own AGENT_TOOLS_ROOT under a temp dir) keeps surfacing as `ship_env` drift until a durable apply repairs it.
- status/apply parity preserved; full pytest suite green.

One edits a relative src/app.py after its execution kernel restarts. The edit must still address its own checkout, not main or the other agent. A file outside any Git repository is a separate case, not automatically a forbidden main-checkout write.

Apply the scenario to the exact operation, code paths and acceptance criteria in the retained description. Record the input, actual result, expected result, source revision and a durable artifact. A failure must be tied to this outcome before reopening; a passing unrelated suite must not close it.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## Problem

`rig apply` writes the machine-level `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/agent-tools/env` (AGENT_TOOLS_ROOT) that every repo's `gh ship` delegator sources when the env var is unset. The root was derived from `agent_tools_source`/`catalog.source` with no guard, so a one-off apply whose source resolved under a temp dir (a mkdtemp clone / $TMPDIR / /tmp — e.g. an agent testing agent-tools from a throwaway worktree) clobbered the durable pointer with a path that vanishes on cleanup.

Observed 2026-07-09 on the CTO's machine:
```
AGENT_TOOLS_ROOT=/private/var/folders/1c/.../T/tmpdhx8hi2a/agent-tools
```
Once the tempdir is gone, `gh ship` exits 127 for EVERY repo on the machine (delegator sources a dead path) until someone manually re-points it. Every merger agent had to override `AGENT_TOOLS_ROOT=/Users/ultra/xp/agent-tools` to ship.

## Evidence / cost of inaction
Recurring silent breakage of the merge path for all agents on the machine; each occurrence costs a manual override and investigation.

## What


## Why (motivation)
After a macOS reboot the LaunchAgent brings tmux up but NO sessions restore. Root cause proven: launchd hands the agent PATH=/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin; the tmux server inherits it; continuum/resurrect run-shell hooks call bare tmux (in /opt/homebrew/bin, not on PATH) -> get_tmux_option @continuum-restore fails -> defaults off -> restore skipped. No StandardOut/ErrPath meant it was invisible.

## User impact
Every reboot loses the user's whole tmux session layout and claude --resume state; the failure is silent (no logs), so it looks like autostart is broken.

## Cost of inaction
Reboots keep dropping all sessions with zero diagnostics; rig re-provisions the same broken, logless autostart on any machine rebuild.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## What


## Why (motivation)
Autosave was dead about a month (last save Jun 16). Root cause proven and fixed in the committed PATH branch: launchd minimal PATH broke continuum init so its status-right autosave hook was never armed. A multi-model brainstorm (Fable claude-fable-5 plus Sol codex gpt-5.6-sol) converged: the PATH fix revives autosave but keeps a six-link fragile chain (status on, interval, PATH, status-right not wiped, tpm not re-init, interpolation alive) with zero observability. A data-protection mechanism must not depend on status-line rendering. An independent launchd saver is immune to that chain, works even on a bad-PATH server, and makes silent death impossible. Sol hardenings for the committed branch: drop the user-writable local bin dir from the plist PATH, use an absolute bash shebang, check the tmux path is a regular executable file not merely existent.

## User impact
Without it, autosave can silently die again on any future environment or config regression and nobody notices for weeks, so a reboot loses all session state. The current PATH fix only re-arms continuum on the NEXT boot and still relies on the fragile status-right mechanism.

## Cost of inaction
The failure class of silent autosave death remains; the next unrelated environment or config change re-breaks it invisibly, exactly as it has repeatedly.

**Illustrative scenario for this concern (not an observed reproduction):** A remote reviewer emits output, then stops. Another remains silent but supplies a trustworthy progress signal. Neither low local CPU nor silence alone identifies quota exhaustion. Preserve partial output, try compatible alternatives where policy permits, and record cancellation/terminal cause without orphaning the owned child.

Apply the scenario to the exact operation, code paths and acceptance criteria in the retained description. Record the input, actual result, expected result, source revision and a durable artifact. A failure must be tied to this outcome before reopening; a passing unrelated suite must not close it.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## What happens

Running `rig apply` on a fully-provisioned machine prints a large plan header — e.g.
`220 action(s)` — immediately followed by a wall of `notes:` lines, then executes with
**no per-action progress** and **no clear completion line**. From the user's seat it looks
like it hangs, and there is no way to tell *what actually changed* or *why* all those notes
are there.

The `notes:` are almost all informational skips, but nothing signals that:

- skills: `opencode auto-loads ~/.agents/skills natively`; `pi uses ~/.config/pi/AGENTS.md`
- autonomous-mode policy notes (review/fix-until-clean, quorum, escalation, `max_agents=4`)
- permissions skipped for `codex` (no allowlist mechanism), `pi` (none), `opencode`
  (glob dialect unverified)
- `hook_bridge: skipped — ... incomplete ... missing plugin.js` (this one is a *real* gap,
  tracked separately — but it's buried in the same undifferentiated wall)

CTO reaction after the last run: "очень неприятный опыт" — a 220-line plan + a wall of
notes with no changed/unchanged breakdown, no progress, and an unclear finish that reads
as a hang.

## Why it's bad

- The plan does not distinguish **what will change** from **what is already converged**
  (idempotent re-affirm). On a converged machine ~all 220 actions are no-ops, but they all
  print identically, so the signal (the 2-3 things that change) drowns in noise.
- Informational notes and real gaps are rendered the same way, so a genuine gap
  (`hook_bridge` skip) is indistinguishable from "opencode loads skills natively, nothing
  to do."
- No progress during apply + no completion summary ⇒ indistinguishable from a hang. (In the
  reported run the process had in fact already exited; there was just no closing line.)

## Proposed fixes

1. **Group the plan by outcome**: `N will change` vs `M already converged (idempotent)`.
   Print the changing actions in full; collapse the converged ones to a count (expandable
   with `--verbose`).
2. **Collapse informational notes** behind a one-line count, e.g.
   `12 notes (informational) — run with --verbose to see them`, and keep only **real gaps**
   inline (the `hook_bridge` skip should read as a WARNING, not sit in the same list as
   "opencode loads skills natively").
3. **Per-action progress during apply** (a running `[k/N] <action>` or a simple spinner/
   counter), so the user can see it is working.
4. **A clear completion line**: `✓ applied N actions in Xs (n changed, m unchanged)` — an
   unambiguous "done" so a finished apply never reads as a hang.
5. **A `--quiet` flag** that suppresses informational notes and converged no-ops, printing
   only changes + real gaps + the completion line.

## Acceptance

- On a converged machine, `rig apply` shows at a glance how many actions changed vs stayed,
  hides informational notes behind a count, surfaces real gaps as warnings, and ends with a
  clear completion line.
- `--quiet` prints only changes, real gaps, and the completion line.
- `--verbose` restores the current full detail.

**Original problem context (historical statement, not a new observation):** PROPOSAL awaiting a decision, not a committed plan. Problem: provisioning a periodic job (for example, a reminders-digest cron entry) hit two real walls today. First, macOS crontab writes require Full Disk Access TCC, which no agent shell process has. Second, a LaunchAgent-install workaround was denied by the Claude Code session's own auto-mode classifier, which treats 'install a persistent scheduled-execution mechanism' as a sensitive action requiring human approval -- arguably correct, since a LaunchAgent runs commands unattended and survives reboots. Net effect: every project that needs a periodic job requires a fresh one-time manual human action (a raw crontab line), with no way for automation to provision it, and this will recur for every future project. Proposed design: rig should provision exactly ONE shared dispatcher on a machine (a single crontab line or LaunchAgent, installed by a HUMAN running 'rig setup' themselves once -- an explicit, narrow, one-time authorized action) that on each tick scans a rig-managed drop-in directory of small per-job definition files and runs wh… [complete text retained below]

**Expected outcomes from this ticket, not invented from its title:**

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## What
PROPOSAL awaiting a decision, not a committed plan. Problem: provisioning a periodic job (for example, a reminders-digest cron entry) hit two real walls today. First, macOS crontab writes require Full Disk Access TCC, which no agent shell process has. Second, a LaunchAgent-install workaround was denied by the Claude Code session's own auto-mode classifier, which treats 'install a persistent scheduled-execution mechanism' as a sensitive action requiring human approval -- arguably correct, since a LaunchAgent runs commands unattended and survives reboots. Net effect: every project that needs a periodic job requires a fresh one-time manual human action (a raw crontab line), with no way for automation to provision it, and this will recur for every future project. Proposed design: rig should provision exactly ONE shared dispatcher on a machine (a single crontab line or LaunchAgent, installed by a HUMAN running 'rig setup' themselves once -- an explicit, narrow, one-time authorized action) that on each tick scans a rig-managed drop-in directory of small per-job definition files and runs whatever job files it finds. After that one-time bootstrap, 'rig apply' for ANY project can register a new periodic job by simply WRITING a job-definition file into that directory -- a plain file write, which agents can already do freely without hitting TCC or the classifier ever again. This mirrors an already-established pattern in this ecosystem: the global-git-hooks skill/pattern (one dispatcher entry point plus a drop-in directory for per-repo hooks) -- just applied to scheduling instead of git hooks. Explicitly noting: this issue is NOT approved or prioritized yet -- it is a design captured for Alex's decision, referencing the concrete pain hit today (2026-07-18, hyperide bug-blitz reminders wiring: a personal-CLI cron.md pm-reminders-push wrapper needed a manual crontab line because of this exact wall).

## Why (motivation)
Every future project that needs a periodic job hits the same two walls (TCC-gated crontab writes, classifier-blocked LaunchAgent installs) and requires a fresh one-time manual human action with no way for automation to provision it on its own.

## User impact
Without a shared dispatcher, every user setting up a new project's scheduled job has to manually edit crontab themselves each time, instead of the tooling (rig apply) just writing a small config file and being done.

## Cost of inaction
This exact friction recurs for every future project that needs a periodic job -- a real one-time-per-project tax on the human, forever, instead of a one-time-per-machine bootstrap.

## What


## Why (motivation)
rig-ecosystem tools (tg-cli, review-cli, rig itself) are developed as live symlinks or long-running daemons — a code change silently has no effect until someone remembers to manually restart the daemon, which wastes debugging time chasing a fix that never actually loaded

## User impact
developers working on rig-ecosystem daemons get instant, zero-manual-step feedback on every commit instead of silently testing stale code

## Cost of inaction

task-cli, the shared ticket-creation CLI used across many repos, already fully implements reading a task: block from a repo's committed rig.yaml file: a repo can declare which issue-tracker backend to use (GitHub Issues or Linear) and how to configure it. The existing reading-side support stays effectively dead in practice despite being fully built and tested, wasting the engineering effort already spent on it, and repos with non-default tracker needs keep silently depending on auto-detection guesswork with no discoverable, supported way to correct a wrong guess.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## Goal

Make Rig able to reconcile many repositories from one command while preserving the same preview-by-default and collect-and-continue semantics as single-repo apply.

This is the missing layer for treating a developer machine or engineering workspace as one managed development environment rather than a set of manually visited repositories.

## Desired UX

```bash
rig fleet apply                         # preview all discovered/registered repos
rig fleet apply commit                  # reconcile all selected repos
rig fleet apply --stack frontend/ts     # only matching stack(s)
rig fleet apply --root ~/work --root ~/xp
rig fleet apply --repo foo --repo bar
```

Selection should support stack/profile, root/path, explicit repo and stable user-defined tags. A blocked/failing target in one repository must not stop unrelated repositories; the final report aggregates errors, warnings, changed/no-op counts, and lint/format finding deltas per repo.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Registry/discovery model for repositories under configured development roots.
- [ ] Preview-by-default; explicit commit performs writes.
- [ ] Selectors for stack/profile, root/path, explicit repo and tags.
- [ ] Global Rig policy + each repository's `rig.yaml` resolve independently before execution.
- [ ] Collect-and-continue across repositories and targets; failures are visible in the final exit/report.
- [ ] Safe bounded parallelism with stable deterministic output.
- [ ] `rig status`/fleet status can summarize drift across the same selection.
- [ ] Machine-readable JSON output for agents/automation.
- [ ] Tests cover mixed stacks, blocked Oxc migration, partial failures and no-op convergence.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## What

`riglib/daily/categorize.py`'s keyword regexes (`_PERF_RE`, `_INFRA_RE`, `_SECURITY_RE`)
scan the ENTIRE PR body text, not just the title/summary. Two concrete miscategorizations
found running `rig daily --since 30d` against real `hyperide/hyper-saas` +
`hyperide/hyper-ext-e2e` merged-PR data on 2026-08-20:

1. **False positive → wrong bucket.** `hyperide/hyper-saas#738` ("wire
   componentPropSurface into a live inspector warning + VS Code parity") is a UI-facing
   Product/UX feature (a Right Sidebar toast). It lands in "Performance" because its body's
   "Deliberately out of scope" section mentions an unrelated follow-up ticket, "HYP-1293
   (ComponentService **perf**/architecture)" — `_PERF_RE`'s `\bperf(ormance)?\b` matches
   that stray word with zero relation to what the PR itself does.
2. **False negative → wrong bucket.** `hyperide/hyper-saas#737` ("fix stale ext-e2e repo
   URL, document known nightly-server gaps") is squarely an infra finding (remote e2e
   server staleness, a silently-skipping nightly cron) but lands in "Other" because
   `_INFRA_RE`'s keyword list (`ci pipeline|github actions|workflow|runner|billing.?block|
deploy(ment)?|release\b|dependency|dependencies|lockfile`) has no term for
   "nightly"/"cron"/"server freshness", and the commit type is `docs`, which isn't in any
   of the type-based buckets either.

## Why (motivation)

Both bugs are two faces of the same root cause: full-body keyword matching over
free-form PR prose is imprecise — it has no way to distinguish "this PR is about X" from
"this PR's body happens to mention the word X in an aside, a follow-up reference, or a
scope-exclusion list." A naive keyword-list patch for #737 (adding "nightly"/"server") 
carries the same risk that produced #738's false positive — it's just as likely to create
a NEW false-positive collision on some future PR that mentions "nightly" in passing.
Fixing this properly needs either narrowing the match window (title + first paragraph
only, not full body) or moving to a lower-confidence-tie-break policy — a real design
change, not a one-line keyword tweak. Deliberately not attempted as a rushed patch on
this merge (see rig-cli#283's own PR discussion).

## User impact

The Slack Daily report occasionally puts a shipped feature/fix under a misleading
heading — a reader skimming just the "Performance" section could think a UI feature was
a performance fix, or a reader skimming "Infra / CI" could miss a real infra item that
landed under "Other" instead. Doesn't affect completeness (every PR still appears
somewhere), only which of the 5 buckets it appears under.

## Cost of inaction

Low — the report is still human-read and short; a misfiled line is easy to visually
correct when pasting into Slack. But it will keep recurring silently on other PRs whose
bodies happen to reference an unrelated ticket/keyword, and nobody will notice unless
they cross-check every line against its actual PR.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Either (a) `categorize()`'s keyword regexes are scoped to a narrower window than the
      full PR body (e.g. title + first paragraph, or excluding "out of scope"/"deferred"
      sections), or (b) an explicit decision is documented for why full-body matching is
      kept and the two known miscategorizations above are accepted as a documented,
      Sibling ticket to rig-cli#281.
- [ ] `hyperide/hyper-saas#738` categorizes as Product / UX, not Performance (regression
      test added to `tests/test_daily_categorize.py` using its real title + a body
      containing the same "perf/architecture" aside).
- [ ] `hyperide/hyper-saas#737` categorizes as Infra / CI, not Other (regression test
      added using its real title + a body mentioning nightly/cron/server-freshness).

Apply the scenario to the exact operation, code paths and acceptance criteria in the retained description. Record the input, actual result, expected result, source revision and a durable artifact. A failure must be tied to this outcome before reopening; a passing unrelated suite must not close it.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

Alex's UX feedback on `rig init` (tg screenshot, 2026-08-25) included: ".git и package manager не инициализируется, стек не настраивается" (.git and the package manager aren't initialized, the stack isn't configured).

Investigated: `rig` has **zero** capability to run `git init`, bootstrap a package manager (npm/pnpm/uv/...), or scaffold a stack. Confirmed via `riglib/detect.py`, `riglib/catalog.py`, `riglib/plan.py`, `riglib/actions/runner.py` — every 'bootstrap'/'init'-adjacent hit in those files is either dependency bootstrap (`doctor.py`) or launchd-agent bootstrap, nothing related to scaffolding a new project.

By `rig`'s own stated mission (this repo's CLAUDE.md): 'a standalone Python CLI that sets up a repo from a committed `rig.yaml` by applying agent-tools content (skills, agent-hooks, git-hook dispatcher, CI gates, MCP) and provisioning the agent harness's auto/permission mode.' The `stack` field (`l1/lang[/framework]`) is a **classification label** used only to select which by-stack skills to install — never a directive to scaffold a project. `rig` DETECTS an existing stack from files already present (package.json, pyproject.toml, go.mod, ...); it was never designed to CREATE one.

For a repo like the one in Alex's screenshot (a fresh landing-page project with no manifest yet), `toolchain: unknown`/`type: unknown` is very likely an ACCURATE report, not a detection bug.

**This is a real product-scope question, not a bug**: does `rig` want to grow into a project-scaffolding tool (run `git init`, pick + bootstrap a package manager, lay down a stack starter) as a genuinely new, separate capability? That's a materially different, larger surface than everything `rig` does today (which only ever touches EXISTING repo state). Recommend: decide explicitly whether this is in scope before anyone builds it — if yes, it likely deserves its own design pass (which stacks/starters, opt-in vs automatic, where the templates live) rather than being bolted onto `rig init`'s TUI as a quick fix.

But there is currently NO way out of a genuinely hung Apply from inside the app -- if a plan action shells out (a skill fetch on a dead network, a `gh` call blocking on an interactive prompt, a hook install waiting on a git lock), the log just stops advancing and 'q'/'x'/ctrl+q are all real no-ops (by design, not a bug) until the action either finishes or the process is killed from another terminal.

Deeper root cause: `riglib/tui/app.py`'s worker threads (`_run_plan_worker`, via `run_worker(..., thread=True)`) have no cooperative cancellation hook -- `run_plan` (in `riglib/actions/runner.py`, outside this PR's diff) isn't given any way to check 'should I stop now'. `call_from_thread` also has no timeout, so if the app were ever torn down while the worker is mid-run (a fatal crash elsewhere, not the normal quit path), the `finally` block's `call_from_thread(self._finish_apply)` could block forever against a dead event loop, and since thread workers are non-daemon (joined at interpreter exit), the whole process could hang on exit.

This needs actual design judgment (not a mechanical fix):
- Should there be a force-quit path (e.g. a second 'q' press within N seconds triggers `os._exit`, after a first press just warns)?
- Should backend subprocesses spawned during a plan run be made non-interactive by default (`stdin=DEVNULL`) and given per-action timeouts, so 'a hook install waits on a TTY prompt forever' can't happen at all?
- Should `run_plan`/the dispatch layer be given an actual cancellation token so a worker CAN be told to stop between actions?

Scoped out of the original UX-fix PR because it requires touching `riglib/actions/runner.py` (untouched by that diff) and involves a real product decision about force-quit UX, not just a bugfix.

## Existing related work

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

Follow-up from PR fixing rig-cli#292 (the `rig init` TUI wizard UX pass).

## Context

That PR added `_atomic_timestamped_backup()` in `riglib/tui/app.py` — an O_CREAT|O_EXCL
atomic name-claim + write-through-the-claimed-fd + inode-verified cleanup, replacing a
`shutil.copy2`-based backup that could silently clobber another writer's backup or follow a
swapped-in symlink. It went through several review rounds and closed a real set of races
(see the function's own docstring for the history). Two classes of finding surfaced during
that hardening that are legitimately out of scope for a UX-fix PR and are tracked here
instead of being silently dropped.

## 1. The hardened backup primitive is TUI-private; the same unhardened bug exists in 3
   other call sites

`_atomic_timestamped_backup` lives in `riglib/tui/app.py` and is used only by the wizard's
Export/Apply buttons. The exact bug it fixes — a second-resolution `<target>.rig-bak-<stamp>`
name with no disambiguator, then a plain `shutil.copy2` — still exists, unfixed, in:

- `riglib/cli.py` — the headless `rig init --config … --yes` persist path
  (`_persist_rig_yaml`). Concrete scenario: a provisioning script runs `rig init --config
  template.yaml --yes` twice within the same second — the second run's backup silently
  overwrites the first, destroying the earliest restore point (the user's original
  hand-edited `rig.yaml`).
- `riglib/actions/fsutil.py` — same check-then-act pattern.
- `riglib/linter_carriers.py` — same check-then-act pattern.

Per the repo's one-engine rule, the atomic primitive should move to a shared stdlib module
(e.g. `riglib/fsutil.py` or wherever makes sense alongside the existing helper there) and all
four call sites should migrate to it.

## 2. Two narrower concurrent-write races remain, even in the hardened TUI path

- Two full wizard/apply instances (not just two `_atomic_timestamped_backup` calls) racing on
  the SAME `rig.yaml`: both back up the old file, both resolve different in-memory states,
  the second writer's config silently overwrites the first's — and neither backup contains
  the lost state, since each only backs up what was on disk before ITS OWN write. Closing
  this needs a repo-scoped write lock around the whole validate→backup→write sequence (not
  just the backup filename), which is a real design question (flock vs lockfile, staleness/
  timeout policy) — this is a systemic property of `state.write()` today, not something the
  backup-name hardening ever claimed to solve, and it applies equally to headless `rig apply`/
  `rig config set`.
- A narrower TOCTOU: `_atomic_timestamped_backup`'s post-write identity check proves the
  backup is intact AT THAT INSTANT, but `_write_config` then proceeds to overwrite the
  original file — a concurrent directory-writer could still unlink/replace the backup in the
  gap between the identity check succeeding and the overwrite, leaving the UI reporting a
  restore point that no longer exists by the time anyone needs it.

Both require an adversary (or another instance) with write access to the same directory
racing very tight windows; low real-world likelihood, but worth a deliberate decision (accept
the current threat-model boundary explicitly, or close it with a lock) rather than leaving it
implicit.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decide whether items in #2 are worth closing now or are an accepted threat-model
      boundary (document the decision either way).
- [ ] If closing #1: the atomic-backup primitive lives in one shared module; `riglib/cli.py`'s
      headless persist path, `riglib/actions/fsutil.py`, and `riglib/linter_carriers.py` all
      use it; a regression test proves two same-second headless `rig init --yes` runs don't
      clobber each other's backup (mirrors `test_export_then_apply_backups_do_not_collide` in
      `tests/test_tui_wizard.py`).

## User impact if not addressed

A user (or an automation script) that runs `rig init` twice in quick succession, or that has
two `rig init`/`rig apply` processes touching the same repo concurrently, can silently lose
their original `rig.yaml` or a config edit with no error and no way to recover it — the tool
reports success (a green checkmark, a "backed up" log line) while the actual data is gone.

## Context

That PR added a version-aware gate so `rig init` refuses to launch the wizard when `textual`
is present but older than the wizard's actual floor (`riglib/doctor.py`'s
`_TEXTUAL_MIN_VERSION`), rather than launching a wizard that then crashes mid-Apply. Over
several review rounds, the three-way classification this needs — "textual is genuinely
absent" vs. "textual is present but too old" vs. "textual is fine" — kept getting
re-implemented slightly differently at each call site, and review caught the same class of
bug (one site's check falling out of sync with another's) more than once:

- a fix that correctly bypassed a distro package manager for a too-old textual accidentally
  bypassed it for a genuinely-absent textual too (dead-coding the OS-level install command);
- a "too old" vs. "missing" diagnosis message that mislabeled one case as the other;
- a PEP-668 remediation-fallback gate computed separately from the install-command builder it
  was meant to mirror, so the two silently drifted.

classification is currently computed independently in at least five places —
`riglib/doctor.py`'s `_python_present`, `_targets_this_interpreter`, and
`_versioned_install_spec`; `riglib/cli.py`'s `_missing_tui_deps`, `_tui_importable`, and
`_setup_preview_no_tui`. `textual_too_old()` (an `importlib.metadata` dist-info read) can run
up to 4-5 times in a single `rig doctor`/`rig init` invocation as a result.

## Suggested fix

Add one function, e.g. `doctor.textual_state() -> Literal["absent", "too_old", "ok"]`, that
owns the guarded `find_spec` check + `textual_too_old()` call exactly once, and have every
call site above consume its result instead of re-deriving the classification. This:

- Eliminates the "one site's guard drifts from another's" bug class structurally instead of
  catching each instance after the fact.
- Cuts the redundant `importlib.metadata` reads.
- Makes the "too old" vs. "missing" message logic in `cli.py` a straightforward `match`/`if`
  on one value instead of parallel boolean computations.

## User impact if not addressed

Not a live bug today (each instance found during review was fixed before merge), but the
duplication is exactly the shape that produces this bug class — a future change to how
"textual is problematic" is defined only needs to be applied in one of five places to
silently drift, and the failure mode (a crash-inducing version treated as fine, or a working
install refused) is user-facing and hard to notice without deliberately re-auditing all five
sites again.

Found while running the FULL `bash tests/smoke.sh` (not just the `--fast` pre-commit
subset) as part of an unrelated PR (rig-cli#292, the `rig init` TUI wizard UX pass) —
confirmed to be pre-existing and unrelated to that PR's diff: it reproduces byte-for-byte
identically with the PR's changes fully `git stash`ed, on the plain branch tip.

## Repro

```
bash tests/smoke.sh
```

fails at the `status nonzero when in sync` check, right after the `rig init --yes --apply`
leg and the idempotent-second-apply leg both pass cleanly. Exit code from `rig status` is 3.

Manually reproducing the same isolated-HOME `rig init --yes --apply` + `rig status`
sequence smoke.sh runs shows the actual drift:

```
GLOBAL — machine-wide (from ~/.config/rig/config.yaml)
  config→disk drift (1) — declared but missing/modified:
    ▸ gh_ship_alias/alias: `gh ship` alias not set (apply sets it so `gh ship <PR>` reaches the ship gate)
```

smoke.sh exports `RIG_GH_ALIAS_DRY_RUN=1` for the whole run (added recently, per its own
comment: "the apply leg would otherwise shell out to a REAL `gh alias set` and rewrite the
developer's actual `gh ship` alias"). That dry-run mode appears to skip the actual
`gh alias set` write (correctly avoiding touching the real machine) but does NOT skip
`rig status`'s later drift check for that same item — so status correctly observes the
alias was never actually written and reports it as drifted, even though the apply "leg"
report showed no error.

Either:
- `rig status` needs to also respect `RIG_GH_ALIAS_DRY_RUN` (treat the item as in-sync when
  dry-run mode is what intentionally skipped writing it), or
- smoke.sh's `status nonzero when in sync` check needs to tolerate the ONE expected
  dry-run-mode drift item rather than asserting a fully clean exit 0.

Whichever direction, `RIG_TMUX_DRY_RUN` and `RIG_TG_CTL_DRY_RUN` (the two sibling dry-run
env vars) do NOT have this problem — smoke's status check passes cleanly with those two
active, so the fix is scoped to whatever `gh_ship_alias` does differently.

## User impact if not addressed

The full `bash tests/smoke.sh` (the CI-run leg, per its own docstring: "CI keeps running
the FULL tests/smoke.sh") fails on every run, on every branch, unrelated to whatever that
branch actually changed — masking a REAL regression in the same run behind a permanent
false-positive red, and eroding trust in the smoke gate — exactly the class of silent-failure
incident the smoke suite exists to prevent (see the file's own header comment on the two
same-day prod failures that motivated it).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `bash tests/smoke.sh` (no `--fast`) passes cleanly on a machine with a real
      agent-tools checkout, with no gh_ship_alias false-positive drift.
- [ ] A regression test (or an adjustment to the existing smoke leg) pins the fix so this
      doesn't silently regress again.

the failing test (`tests/test_cli.py::test_codex_update_cli_missing_updater_returns_127`) is
about the `codex update` subcommand, a completely different feature area than anything
rig-cli#292 touches (doctor/textual-version-gating/TUI wizard).

## Repro

```
python -m pytest -q
```

Failed ONCE out of three consecutive full-suite runs during a heavy-CPU-load period (several
concurrent `review diff` multi-model review passes were running on the same machine at the
time). The test passes reliably in isolation (`pytest tests/test_cli.py::test_codex_update_cli_missing_updater_returns_127`)
and on the two other full-suite runs taken minutes apart.

Failure:
```
E       assert 8 == 127
```

## Likely cause

The test at `tests/test_cli.py:93` passes `--probe-timeout 0.5` (a real, hardcoded
500-millisecond timeout) to `main(["codex", "update", ...])`, which spawns a REAL bash
subprocess (`live`, a fake `codex` binary script) and expects the probe to specifically time
out, producing exit code 127. Under system load (CPU contention from other processes), the
subprocess can plausibly take long enough to hit a DIFFERENT code path (an actual response,
or a different failure classification) within or around that tight window, producing a
different exit code (8, observed) instead of the expected 127 timeout code.

## User impact if not addressed

An intermittent, load-sensitive false-positive test failure that can block or confuse CI runs
and local pre-commit gates unrelated to whatever the actual change under test is -- eroding
trust in the suite the same way the smoke-gate false positives described in
`tests/smoke.sh`'s own header comment do.

## Suggested fix

Either raise the hardcoded probe timeout to something with more slack under load (e.g. 2-3s),
or make the test deterministic without depending on wall-clock timing at all (e.g. inject a
fake/controllable clock or a way to force the "not responding" classification synchronously
rather than racing a real subprocess against a real timeout).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The test no longer depends on winning a real-subprocess-vs-wall-clock race under
      variable system load, or the timeout has enough margin that this doesn't reproduce
      under realistic CI/dev-machine load.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## Context

Flagged by the GitHub-integrated Codex review bot on PR #306 (the rig-cli#292 TUI wizard
fix). Verified pre-existing and unrelated to that PR's diff: `run_wizard()` in
`riglib/tui/app.py` is untouched by #306's changes and reads identically on `main`:

```python
def run_wizard(repo_root: Path, stack: str | None = None) -> int:
    app = _build_wizard_class()(repo_root, stack=stack)
    app.run()
    return 0
```

## The gap

`app.run()`'s return value is discarded, and the function unconditionally returns `0`. If
`run_plan` raises partway through an Apply (some actions already executed, then an
unexpected I/O error or similar), the wizard's Apply handler logs the failure to the
in-app RichLog and re-enables the controls (recoverable UI state -- this part works
correctly), but once the user quits the wizard, `rig init`'s process exit code is still
`0` -- a shell script or CI job driving `rig init` non-interactively-adjacent (e.g. wrapped
in an expect-style harness, or checking `$?` after the terminal session) would see success
even though the apply only partially completed.

## Suggested fix

Track whether any Apply run inside the session ended in failure (a simple instance flag,
set in the same place `_finish_apply`/the worker's error path already logs to the RichLog),
and have `run_wizard()` inspect it after `app.run()` returns, propagating a nonzero exit
code when it's set. Needs a decision on scope: does a user-initiated quit WITHOUT ever
running an Apply count as success (probably yes), and does quitting mid-Apply (before it
resolves either way) count as a failure or an incomplete-but-not-erroring exit (needs
product judgment, not just an engineering call).

## User impact if not addressed

A script or agent driving `rig init` interactively cannot rely on the process exit code to
detect a partial/failed apply -- it has to parse the TUI's log output instead, which is not
a stable machine-readable contract.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `rig init`'s process exit code reflects whether the wizard's Apply run(s) ended in
      failure, not just whether the process itself ran without crashing.
- [ ] A regression test drives a real (or realistically faked) `run_plan` failure through the
      wizard and asserts the exit code `run_wizard()` returns is nonzero.

(3) Make an edit interactive instead of silently writing-only: after an edit (or batch), show a computed plan preview (mirrors rig apply info, via the shared riglib/plan.py build() + riglib/actions/runner.py run_plan()), let the user confirm or skip individual actions (matched by a stable key, not index, to survive re-plans), then show live per-phase apply progress via a polling job endpoint (background thread + run_plan's existing on_start/progress callbacks -- the concept PR #306 shipped for the rig init TUI, reused here for the web UI, not the Textual-specific mechanism). Apply is serialized process-wide (one job at a time, 409 on a second start) and staleness-checked (a hash of the previewed action-key-set sent back with the apply POST; mismatch is refused) so nothing applies a plan the user did not actually see. (4) Every planned action in the preview and progress views carries a visual tag/badge naming its real kind, driven by a new riglib/action_tags.py registry mapping every riglib/actions/runner.py _HANDLERS kind to one of a small set of real categories (creates file, edits file, symlinks, installs hook, changes permission/guard, starts/reloads service, remote GitHub change, declares policy only/no disk effect, installs system tool), each naming exactly where on disk (or which remote setting) it touches and whether the effect lands on running agents or on the human's own workflow. A test asserts the tag registry's keys equal runner._HANDLERS's keys so a newly added action kind can never ship untagged. This breaks the module's stated invariant that config-web never runs rig apply -- every write endpoint keeps and documents the full existing CSRF/host/content-type/body-cap guard stack as the new security boundary, and the module docstring, the CLAUDE.md config-web paragraph, and the config-web --help text are all updated in the same change to describe the new behavior.

## Why (motivation)
config-web today only edits one repo's rig.yaml at a time (whichever -C pointed at when it started) and an edit only writes the config file -- it never runs rig apply, so a checkbox click looks like it did nothing real. The user asked for it to become a real machine console: every rig-managed repo in one place, a Global-config-only tab, a drift panel so config-vs-disk mismatches are visible without a separate rig status run, and turning the silent write-only edit into a full preview-confirm-apply flow with live progress.

## User impact
Alex (and anyone else on the machine) can open one local page, see every rig-managed repo plus the global config, see real drift instead of guessing, and actually apply a change from the browser with a plan preview and live progress instead of a checkbox that silently only half-works and then requires a separate terminal round-trip to apply.

## Cost of inaction
config-web stays a partial, confusing tool: it looks like a control panel but a click only writes a file with no visible effect, drift is invisible without leaving the page, and there is no machine-wide view -- so people keep bypassing it and running rig apply commit by hand, and the shipped web UI accrues zero real usage relative to the build cost already sunk into it.

- [x] rig config-web run with no -C, started in a repo with a committed rig.yaml, shows a tab bar with a tab for that repo plus every non-stale repo in ~/.config/rig/repositories.json that has a rig.yaml, plus a Global tab; switching tabs re-renders that scope's areas/fields with no page reload — forced: Verified via automated tests, not a screenshot: tests/test_config_web_scopes.py (discover_scopes finds every non-stale registry repo with a rig.yaml + Global scope) and tests/test_config_web_endpoints.py (page renders the tab bar via build_html/_tab_bar). PR #318 merged (fdf01ba).
- [x] the Global tab's model is built via cfg.load(repo_root, include_repo=False) -- editing a GLOBAL-only option there never reads or writes any repo rig.yaml — forced: Verified via tests/test_config_web.py::test_build_model_global_only_omits_repo_layer_areas and test_build_model_global_only_never_reads_repo_rigyaml (cfg.load(repo_root, include_repo=False) confirmed, malformed repo rig.yaml doesn't break the Global tab). PR #318 merged (fdf01ba).
- [x] GET /api/drift?scope=<id> returns the same DriftReport riglib/drift.py detect() would produce for that scope's plan (config-vs-disk missing AND disk-vs-config extra, both directions, never auto-reconciled), rendered as a panel next to the settings; the initial page GET does not block on it — forced: Verified via tests/test_config_web_endpoints.py::test_handle_drift_reports_missing_before_apply and tests/test_config_web_plan.py's compute_scope_drift tests -- GET /api/drift?scope=<id> returns the same DriftReport riglib/drift.py's compute_drift_report (shared with rig status) produces, rendered next to settings via loadDrift() in config_web.py. - Add a single-flight lock (or atomic clone-then-rename) around the tmux plugin clone step in _tmux_activate so two concurrent 'rig apply' invocations can never delete each other's in-progress or completed plugin clone
- Add a regression test simulating two concurrent tmux-plugin-clone attempts and asserting neither destroys the other's successful clone

## Existing related work

[agent-tools#476](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/476), [agent-tools#495](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/495), [rig-cli#202](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/202), [rig-cli#327](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/327), [rig-cli#355](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/355), [rig-cli#461](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/461). These are observed references, not automatically asserted blocking dependencies.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## What
Alex has asked multiple times for a full investigation into why non-Claude-Code harnesses (Codex, opencode/oc, omp) get weaker support than Claude Code in rig, plus containerized proof of cross-harness behavior using Apple's native 'container' CLI (v1.0.0, confirmed installed and working; not Docker). This ticket records the completed investigation (concrete file:line gap catalog below) and specifies the containerized test-matrix design to build next, extending the existing Docker-based clean-room e2e (tests/test_cleanroom_e2e.py) to run parametrized across harness kind using 'container' instead of 'docker'.

GAP CATALOG (file:line references, riglib in rig-cli unless noted):
1. Auto-mode / permission-mode write is Claude-Code-only. riglib/actions/runner.py:724-726 (_HARNESS_MODE_KEY dict) has exactly one entry: {'claude-code': ('permissions', 'defaultMode')}. desired_harness_value() (runner.py:895-903) looks this up and raises KeyError for any other kind, so riglib/plan.py only ever emits the apply_harness action for claude-code; codex/opencode/omp/pi/commandcode silently get no auto-mode write at all beyond a plan note.
2. The shared agents-hooks/v1 bridge (the thing that makes worktree_only, orchestrator_only, block-raw-pr-merge, block-reset-hard etc. actually fire) has NO omp entry anywhere. riglib/plan.py:1433-1448 (_HOOK_BRIDGE_HARNESSES) lists claude-code, codex, opencode only. Confirmed this is not just a rig-cli wiring gap: agent-tools/lib/ ships cc_hook_bridge/, codex_hook_bridge/, opencode_hook_bridge/ but no omp_hook_bridge/ at all. riglib/plan.py:1503-1513 (_build_hook_bridge_for_kind) silently returns for an unsupported kind and ONLY appends a plan note if the user explicitly set harness.hook_bridge.enabled=true for that kind (the default-on case stays quiet, per the comment at plan.py:1508-1511) -- so a machine running omp as its harness (Alex's own daily driver per [rig-cli#202](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/202)) gets zero indication that worktree_only/orchestrator_only never fire for it. omp instead gets only its own separate, narrower TS guard extension (riglib/permissions.py HARNESS_GUARD/HARNESS_APPROVAL, ~line 343 and ~377) covering a fixed deny/ask baseline (force-push, sudo rm, pkill, reset --hard) -- this is real enforcement but NOT the same rule set as the shared agent-hooks catalog, and specifically does not include worktree_only or orchestrator_only.
3. Where a bridge DOES exist (opencode), the shared hook LOGIC does not match the harness's own tool-call schema, so hooks don't block the dangerous thing, they deadlock the whole session. Already found and root-caused: [agent-tools#495](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/495) (background-subagent-gate demands Claude-Code-only fields opencode's Task tool schema rejects, so every non-trivial dispatch is blocked) and [agent-tools#476](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/476) (opencode sessions have no authoritative per-session identity, so delegation gates misclassify every opencode session as 'the orchestrator', forcing manual approval on every gated command). Real fixes already exist in open, UNSHIPPED pull requests [agent-tools#499](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/499) and [agent-tools#497](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/497) -- these need to land, this ticket does not duplicate that work.
4. Per-command allowlists, guard extensions, and execpolicy files are each a genuinely different, harness-appropriate mechanism, not one gap: riglib/permissions.py HARNESS_ALLOWLISTS (~line 148) covers claude-code (array) + opencode (object) only; HARNESS_ALLOWLIST_NA (~line 166) explicitly documents why codex/pi/omp/commandcode have no equivalent (codex uses its own execpolicy .rules mechanism instead, HARNESS_EXECPOLICY ~line 700; omp uses the guard extension instead). This part of the system is intentionally per-harness and mostly well-designed -- the gap catalog above (items 1-3) is the real second-class-citizen problem, not this family.
5. A live, separate, currently-being-fixed bug in agent-tools/lib/codex_hook_bridge/dispatch.py: the Stop-hook event translation may not expose a stable per-session identifier the way cc_hook_bridge does for Claude Code (_ID_KEYS at dispatch.py:28, Stop handling at dispatch.py:38). Another agent is actively fixing this specific bug right now; noted here only as one more concrete example of the class of gap this ticket catalogs, not duplicated.
6. No container/VM-based regression test proves ANY of the above today. tests/test_cleanroom_e2e.py (RIG_CLEANROOM_E2E=1, Docker-based) is the only real fresh-environment e2e that exists, and it only ever configures harness.kind: claude-code -- it has never been parametrized across harness kind, and it uses 'docker', not Apple's 'container'.

CONTAINER-MATRIX DESIGN (Apple 'container' CLI, not Docker):
Extend the tests/test_cleanroom_e2e.py pattern (fresh non-root user, empty $HOME, self-contained fake agent-tools checkout, real CLI run, in-container assertion script) to run under Apple's 'container' CLI (confirmed: 'container build -t <tag> <context-dir>' and 'container run --rm <image>' both exist and match the docker build/run shape closely enough to adapt directly; 'container image rm/delete' replaces 'docker image rm -f'). Parametrize the harness.kind in the generated rig.yaml fixture across claude-code / codex / opencode / omp, and assert per kind: (a) skills are discoverable the way that kind expects (riglib/harness_skills.py's three discovery families), (b) the auto-mode/permission write happens for claude-code and is a documented, visible skip for the others (see gap 1), (c) the agents-hooks bridge registers for claude-code/codex/opencode and is a documented, visible skip for omp (see gap 2) until agent-tools ships an omp_hook_bridge, (d) for opencode specifically, once agent-tools#499/#497 ship, a live worktree_only or orchestrator_only parity assertion actually blocks/allows the same way claude-code does. KNOWN OPEN TECHNICAL QUESTION, verified live on this machine (container CLI 1.0.0): 'container run' has no documented 'docker run --network none' equivalent -- 'container run --help' only shows '--network <name>' to attach a named network, with no offline/none mode listed. The clean-room test's fully-offline-in-container invariant (test_cleanroom_e2e.py's own stated design goal) needs a verified replacement mechanism (omitting --network entirely and confirming no default egress, or another isolation approach) before the container variant can claim the same guarantee -- do not assume parity with Docker's --network none without checking this first.

## Why (motivation)
Alex has raised this repeatedly, most recently in frustration that a full investigation and containerized proof still had not happened despite multiple prior requests. Separately, Alex and a collaborator (Denny) are planning to integrate this rig ecosystem with Denny's own 'axe' agent-management system to build a combined agent development platform -- an unverified, harness-inconsistent guard layer becomes the shared foundation two teams would build on if this stays unresolved. [rig-cli#327](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/327) already opened part of this ask (container tests for two specific guards on opencode/omp) but has sat as an open ticket with real linked agent-tools bugs and unshipped fixes, without the Codex coverage, the Apple 'container' tooling, or the broader auto-mode/hook-bridge-registration gaps this investigation found.

## User impact
omp is Alex's own daily-driver harness (per [rig-cli#202](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/202)), yet none of the shared safety rules apply to it today: the rule that keeps an agent from editing code outside a separate work branch, the rule that stops the main coordinating agent from editing code directly instead of delegating to a sub-agent, and the rule against dangerous git commands (force-push, hard reset) from the shared rule set simply do not run for omp sessions, and rig does not tell anyone this is happening unless they go looking. Codex and opencode sessions get partial coverage, and opencode's coverage is known to actively freeze a session (block every possible action, not just the dangerous one) until two already-written fixes ship. Nobody today has automated, repeatable proof that a safety rule behaves the same way regardless of which of the four supported harnesses someone is running -- every future change to these rules risks silently breaking on three of the four harnesses, undetected until a real incident.

## Cost of inaction
The same requests keep resurfacing as verbal asks instead of tracked, completed engineering work -- this investigation itself exists because Alex asked how many times already. The omp gap stays invisible because rig currently only prints a warning about it when a user explicitly turns the hook bridge on for omp, which almost nobody will do. As the rig ecosystem moves toward integrating with Denny's axe agent-management system, the unverified and inconsistent guard behavior across harnesses becomes baked into whatever the two systems build together, making it far more expensive to fix later.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A written gap catalog (this ticket's body) enumerates every place in rig-cli's reconciler where a harness kind is special-cased, with exact file:line references, distinguishing genuinely-not-applicable cases (documented, e.g. codex's execpolicy standing in for an allowlist) from silent-gap cases (e.g. omp has no agents-hooks bridge at all).
- [ ] A container-based test, built on Apple's 'container' CLI following the pattern already proven in tests/test_cleanroom_e2e.py, provisions a fresh non-root user with an empty home directory and runs a real 'rig apply' for each of claude-code, codex, opencode, and omp as the configured harness kind.
- [ ] That test asserts, per harness kind: skills are discoverable the way that harness expects, the auto-mode/permission-mode write happens or is a visible documented skip, and the shared agent-hooks bridge either registers correctly or is a visible documented skip -- never a silent one.
- [ ] At least one harness (recommend opencode, since agent-tools#499 and agent-tools#497 already contain unshipped fixes) has a passing parity assertion proving a specific shared guard (worktree_only or orchestrator_only) blocks/allows identically to claude-code, or the ticket explicitly records why it cannot yet and what it is blocked on.
- [ ] The container-run network-isolation question (Apple 'container' has no documented docker-run---network-none equivalent) is resolved with a verified mechanism before the test suite claims an offline guarantee.
- [ ] The default-silent omp hook-bridge skip (riglib/plan.py, the note that only surfaces when harness.hook_bridge.enabled is explicitly set) is either fixed so rig status always surfaces it, or explicitly deferred with Alex's sign-off, since silent gaps contradict this repo's own drift-is-never-silent rule.
- [ ] Ticket cross-references rig-cli#327 (linked above) and records that shipping this ticket's container-matrix work satisfies #327's acceptance criteria, so #327 can close without duplicated effort.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## What


## Why (motivation)
Independent multi-model review of agent-tools PR #439 (the subagent-no-monitor hook) found that CC only applies its own 600s default PreToolUse hook timeout, because _bridge_block in riglib/actions/runner.py never writes a timeout field into any matcher's settings.json block -- for ANY of the existing matchers (Bash, Edit/Write/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit, Agent/Task, Skill), not just the new Monitor one. subagent-no-bg-longproc's own pre-bash descriptor already declares timeout_ms 960000 (900s tg-ctl cap plus a 30s margin) specifically so a hung Telegram approval resolves before the descriptor's own on_error policy could kick in -- but since CC kills the bridge subprocess at 600s regardless, that safety margin has never actually been reachable for any hatch-using pre-bash hook shipped so far. This is a pre-existing condition, not something this diff introduced, but the same race now also applies unchanged to the new Monitor matcher.

## User impact
A person who is asked for a one-time Telegram approval on a background agent's request, and who takes more than 10 minutes to notice and respond, can end up with the agent silently proceeding as if the request had failed and been denied, or as if it had been approved, depending on which failure path the interrupted process happens to take -- rather than getting the clear deny-by-default behavior the approval flow is supposed to guarantee.

## Cost of inaction
Every hatch-using hook that goes through this bridge keeps carrying a documented safety margin (a timeout_ms comfortably above the tg-ctl worst case) that can never actually be exercised, because Claude Code silently overrides it with its own shorter default -- a false sense of safety that a future incident investigation would have to rediscover from scratch.

## Worked verification example

### Ticket-specific check

**Operation under review:** worktree gc: a process that exits mid-scan marks every worktree as live (pid race in the liveness snapshot).

**Original problem context (historical statement, not a new observation):** The liveness snapshot in [riglib/worktree_gc.py](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/blob/main/riglib/worktree_gc.py) (`_live_process_cwds`) runs `pgrep` to collect agent pids, then one `lsof` per pid to read its cwd. When a pid exits between those two calls, `lsof` fails for it and the code treats that as 'cannot verify', degrading the WHOLE snapshot to 'everything is live'. A pid that vanished is by definition not live. Fix: after an `lsof` failure re-check the pid with `os.kill(pid, 0)`; ESRCH (no such process) means 'not live, continue'; any other outcome (pid still alive but lsof failed, lsof missing) stays fail-safe as today. Found by the live dry-run of the gc implementation shipped in [PR #347](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/pull/347); follow-up to [rig-cli#329](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/329).

**Expected outcomes from this ticket, not invented from its title:**
- A hermetic test fakes `pgrep` returning a pid and `lsof` failing for it with the pid gone (os.kill raises ProcessLookupError); `_live_process_cwds()` returns a trusted list (not None) that excludes the vanished pid, and no 'liveness check could not be verified' warning is printed.
- A hermetic test fakes `pgrep` returning a pid and `lsof` failing for it while the pid is still alive (os.kill succeeds); `_live_process_cwds()` still returns None (fail-safe: every worktree treated as live) and prints the stderr warning.
- A hermetic test: `lsof` raising OSError (binary missing) for a live pid still degrades the snapshot to None.
- The unit suite (pytest) and the fast smoke gate ([tests/smoke.sh](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/blob/main/tests/smoke.sh) with --fast) are green; the module stays stdlib-only at import time.
