One edits a relative src/app.py after its execution kernel restarts. The edit must still address its own checkout, not main or the other agent. A file outside any Git repository is a separate case, not automatically a forbidden main-checkout write.

Apply the scenario to the exact operation, code paths and acceptance criteria in the retained description. Record the input, actual result, expected result, source revision and a durable artifact. A failure must be tied to this outcome before reopening; a passing unrelated suite must not close it.

## Existing related work

[rig-cli#329](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/329). These are observed references, not automatically asserted blocking dependencies.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## What
The liveness snapshot in [riglib/worktree_gc.py](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/blob/main/riglib/worktree_gc.py) (`_live_process_cwds`) runs `pgrep` to collect agent pids, then one `lsof` per pid to read its cwd. When a pid exits between those two calls, `lsof` fails for it and the code treats that as 'cannot verify', degrading the WHOLE snapshot to 'everything is live'. A pid that vanished is by definition not live. Fix: after an `lsof` failure re-check the pid with `os.kill(pid, 0)`; ESRCH (no such process) means 'not live, continue'; any other outcome (pid still alive but lsof failed, lsof missing) stays fail-safe as today. Found by the live dry-run of the gc implementation shipped in [PR #347](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/pull/347); follow-up to [rig-cli#329](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/329).

## Why (motivation)
The gc implementer's own live dry-run over ~/xp reported 4 removable entries (~1.86 GB) while an independent pass minutes later reported 8 (~2.2 GB). The difference was exactly two repos (`gitapp`, `hyperos-handoff`) marked live by pids that had already exited. The fail-safe direction is right for genuine uncertainty, but a vanished process is not uncertainty — it is certainty that nothing is running there.

## User impact
Alex runs `rig worktree gc` to reclaim disk from ~70 stale worktrees. Today gc refuses to clean worktrees that are actually free because some agent process happened to exit during the scan — on a busy machine (agents starting and stopping constantly) that happens on most runs, so the report under-counts what can be removed and the cleanup leaves gigabytes behind with a misleading 'live agent found here' reason.

## Cost of inaction
Every gc run on a busy machine is non-deterministic: the removable set shrinks by whatever pids happened to exit during the ~1s scan, the reported reason ('a running process was found there') is false for those entries, and the disk sprawl [rig-cli#329](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/329) was filed to fix stays partly unreclaimed with no signal to the user about why.

- [x] A hermetic test: `lsof` raising OSError (binary missing) for a live pid still degrades the snapshot to None. — proof: ![proof](/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ultra-xp-rig-cli/89e7f5e9-4808-41e8-bf8b-0a8b213b7c89/scratchpad/proof-1-3-liveness-tests.txt)
- [x] The unit suite (pytest) and the fast smoke gate ([tests/smoke.sh](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/blob/main/tests/smoke.sh) with --fast) are green; the module stays stdlib-only at import time. — proof: ![proof](/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ultra-xp-rig-cli/89e7f5e9-4808-41e8-bf8b-0a8b213b7c89/scratchpad/proof-4-suite-smoke.txt)

**Expected outcomes from this ticket, not invented from its title:**
- An opt-in pytest module (RIG_CONTAINER_E2E=1) runs the rig clean-room end to end on Apple's native container CLI, once per harness kind, inside a container with no network egress and a brand-new empty HOME. Auto-skips when the container CLI or its system service is absent, and refuses to build under 3 GB free disk.
- For each of claude-code, codex, opencode and omp the run proves: rig init --yes --apply succeeds; skills are discoverable the way that harness expects; agent-hook descriptors, the git-hook dispatcher and the CI workflows are installed; the permission-mode write and the agents-hooks bridge either happened or are visibly noted in rig apply info, so a silent skip fails the test; a second rig apply changes nothing; and rig status exits 0.
- The real worktree-only-writes hook blocks a write on the default branch and allows the same write in a feature worktree, driven through that harness's own bridge dispatcher.
- Where the harness binary can run headless and offline, a REAL harness session driven by an in-container stub model provider hits a guarded action and is blocked by the bridge. Any harness that genuinely cannot do this records a labelled, reasoned fallback instead of a result dressed up as a live session.

## Why (motivation)
The parent ticket [rig-cli#337](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/337) recorded that codex, opencode and omp are second-class harnesses and named a container-based cross-harness parity matrix as the outstanding deliverable. The existing Docker clean-room only ever exercises harness kind claude-code, so every gap in the other three kinds is invisible to the test suite. ## Why (motivation)

The config-web Global tab cannot remedy it: it renders only GLOBAL-writable areas and rejects these options as repo-layer. The PR shipped without this fix because rig was broken machine-wide ([rig-cli 365](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/365)) until it merged; the documented remedy (rig config set --global skills.known ...) works today.

## User impact
A user who follows the rig status remedy through the wizard or the config-web instead of the CLI silently hides the global known-list and gets the drift wall back for that repo, with a committed rig.yaml that lists machine-specific skills.

## Cost of inaction
The provenance feature is only reachable correctly through one of the four editing surfaces; the wizard and the config-web write a machine-specific list into a committed file, which then lies to every other machine that clones the repo.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] Editing skills.known, agent_hooks.known or mcp.known through rig setup or the config-web writes the GLOBAL config (~/.config/rig/config.yaml), never a repo rig.yaml; ci.known stays in the repo file. The config-web Global tab shows these three options. — proof: ![proof](/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ultra-xp-rig-cli/89e7f5e9-4808-41e8-bf8b-0a8b213b7c89/scratchpad/proof-372-ac1-routing-and-global-tab.log)

## Why (motivation)
On the reference machine rig apply commit --yes printed '0 changed' and its verify step printed '20/20 sampled matched dirs carry .metadata_never_index', while rig status run immediately afterwards printed '65/2500 dependency/build dirs lack .metadata_never_index'. Alex cannot trust either command: rig apply claims the machine is converged, rig status contradicts it a second later, and there is no way to tell a harmless just-created cache directory from a directory the sweep actually failed to cover. title: git-hooks dispatcher: install and drift-check review-gate from the installed review-cli, not the agent-tools copy
body:
## What
rig's [git-hooks dispatcher action](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/blob/main/riglib/actions/runner.py) copies the review-gate composer from agent-tools, while review-cli ships the up-to-date gate body (trivial-delta tolerance from [review-cli#211](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/211), merge skip from [review-cli#396](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/issues/396)). Make rig source the review-gate body from 'review install-commit-hook --print-gate' when review is installed (agent-tools copy as fallback), install it per-file so a re-apply stays a no-op, and have rig status report drift when the installed gate differs from what the installed review-cli prints.

## Why (motivation)
The commit gate forces full reviews on one-line fixes and blocks merges, so agents loop or bypass it with --no-verify; the fix shipped in review-cli never reached the installed gate because rig installs a different copy.

## User impact
Alex and every coding agent: after this, a fixed gate reaches the machine with the next rig apply, and rig status tells Alex when the installed gate is stale instead of agents discovering it through 3-4 wasted review rounds.

## Cost of inaction
The installed gate silently stays a stale fork; every future gate fix in review-cli is invisible on the machine until someone diffs the files by hand.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] rig apply commit writes ~/.config/git/hooks/review-gate equal to the output of review install-commit-hook --print-gate; a second apply reports the composers as skipped/unchanged
- [ ] rig status reports git-hooks drift when the installed review-gate differs from the review-cli output, and in sync after rig apply commit
- [ ] the unit suite never shells out to a real review binary (env seam, autouse fixture); a fake review script proves both install and drift

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- PR: https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/pull/386
- Merge commit: https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/commit/0e231117e38af4f074b07fcb00ea7fd807e6db12

## Skipped gates
- post-merge-acceptance: Criteria 1-2 require live rig apply on operator machine with review-cli installed; CI unit+integration tests prove install/drift logic; post-merge: operator runs rig apply commit once to refresh global review-gate
- screenshots: CLI change, no UI
- user-impact-quality: impact names who (Alex + agents) and what changes for them

title: rig apply provisions ~/.bunfig.toml isolated linker + globalStore so every bun install shares one package tree
body:
## What
bun install on this machine copies/clonefiles every package into each project's node_modules. 91 hyperide git worktrees each showed about 1 GiB node_modules with nlink=1 and distinct inodes. Parent du of the Claude worktrees directory under hyperide was 43 GiB. There is no ~/.bunfig.toml. Bun's documented fix is isolated linker plus globalStore (https://bun.sh/docs/pm/global-store) which materializes packages once under the bun cache links directory and makes each node_modules a few megabytes of symlinks. rig already provisions machine-wide files (gitignore block, spotlight). It does not yet write bunfig. Add a GLOBAL-only opt-in bun block that rig apply reconciles into ~/.bunfig.toml, rig status reports drift, and verify checks the two keys.

## Why (motivation)
Worktree-heavy agent work multiplies node_modules by N. bun's default (hoisted, globalStore off) clonefile-copies into every tree even when the download cache is warm. The disk fills and the next bun install in a new worktree does it again.

## User impact
When you create another git worktree and run bun install, packages should appear as symlinks into a single machine store instead of another gigabyte copy. Disk stays shared across projects. Warm reinstalls after deleting node_modules become symlink-only.

## Cost of inaction
Every new agent worktree keeps paying a full node_modules copy. The 43 GiB hyperide pattern repeats on the next repo. A hand-written bunfig drifts from the rest of the machine config and is invisible to rig status.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] With bun.enabled true in the global config, rig apply writes or updates ~/.bunfig.toml so install.linker is isolated and install.globalStore is true, and a second apply is a no-op when already correct. Proof: `tests/test_bunfig.py` (`test_managed_block_sets_isolated_linker_and_global_store`, `test_apply_creates_then_skips`) — 26 passed. PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/pull/441 — forced: non-visual CLI: tests/test_bunfig.py 26 passed; du/inode proof in PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/pull/441 (du -sh node_modules 0B/0B symlink trees; ms inode 636274660 nlink=6; picocolors inode 636274665 nlink=9)
- [x] rig status reports bunfig drift when the file is missing or those two keys are wrong, and reports nothing bun-related when bun.enabled is false. Proof: `tests/test_bunfig.py::test_plan_emits_bunfig_action_only_when_enabled` (no action when disabled); drift wired via `_check_bunfig`. PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/pull/441 — forced: non-visual CLI: tests/test_bunfig.py 26 passed; du/inode proof in PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/pull/441 (du -sh node_modules 0B/0B symlink trees; ms inode 636274660 nlink=6; picocolors inode 636274665 nlink=9)
- [x] A pre-existing ~/.bunfig.toml that already has extra user keys AND the two required values is left untouched; a pre-existing file that lacks them is a conflict (or backup-then-write per on_conflict), never a silent clobber of unrelated tables. Proof: `tests/test_bunfig.py::test_resolve_handwritten_with_both_keys_is_ok_without_taking_ownership`, `test_resolve_existing_install_table_without_linker_is_conflict`, `test_apply_does_not_clobber_existing_install_table`. — forced: non-visual CLI: tests/test_bunfig.py 26 passed; du/inode proof in PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/pull/441 (du -sh node_modules 0B/0B symlink trees; ms inode 636274660 nlink=6; picocolors inode 636274665 nlink=9)
- [x] Hermetic tests cover create, skip, conflict, and disabled; config-schema docs document the bun block in the same commit. **Operation under review:** Add rig env set/list/del for global env.vars keys.

**Original problem context (historical statement, not a new observation):** There is no `rig env` command. ## Worked verification example

### Ticket-specific check

**Operation under review:** rig never provisions an EnterWorktree permission entry, so every worktree entry into the canonical .worktrees/ path prompts.

**Original problem context (historical statement, not a new observation):** CORRECTED DESIGN (superseding the original "broadly allow EnterWorktree" framing, Alex 2026-09-08): EnterWorktree's own tool description says it "Creates an isolated worktree (via git or configured hooks) and switches the session into it" -- it can itself create a worktree at a model-supplied path, not merely switch into a pre-existing one. Broadly trusting EnterWorktree via a static permissions.allow entry would therefore open the exact same location-bypass hole (a worktree landing outside <repo>/.worktrees/, GH-329's failure mode) that agent-tools PR#610 (block-raw-worktree-add, agent a3105ae878f4afee3) closes for the git-argv-level case (git worktree add/remove/move). A blanket EnterWorktree permission grant would let a caller route around that same guard through a different tool. The fix must be PATH-SCOPED, not broad: - A target under the canonical, rig-sanctioned <repo>/.worktrees/<name> -> auto-allow, no interactive prompt (this is the actual friction rig-cli#418 exists to remove). - A target anywhere else -> stays gated (prompt, or deny/hatch-escalate, mirroring block-raw-wor… [complete text retained below]

**Expected outcomes from this ticket, not invented from its title:**
- Rig's baseline permission provisioning learns EnterWorktree as a known permission key and provisions a sensible default allow rule during rig apply for every configured harness kind that supports it, mirroring how other baseline tool permissions are already provisioned
- The provisioned rule is scoped sensibly -- broadly trusting EnterWorktree is reasonable given the actual cross-agent-worktree-entry security concern is already handled by the enterworktree-foreign-guard agent-hook (a separate layer), but document that reasoning inline in the permission entry per this repo's own house rule that every permission/agent-hook toggle needs an inline comment explaining what it is for and what it does NOT weaken
- rig status reports drift if a repo's settings file is missing this baseline entry, same as it does for other rig-managed permission baselines
- Regression test: a fresh rig apply on a clean config provisions the EnterWorktree allow rule; rig status on a config missing it reports drift; re-apply is idempotent

Re-run these checks at the recorded source revision; keep setup, actual output and result for each criterion separate. Historical checked boxes below are retained as history, not re-checked by this text.



**Illustrative scenario for this concern (not an observed reproduction):** Two agents work on the same repository in different .worktrees directories. One edits a relative src/app.py after its execution kernel restarts. The edit must still address its own checkout, not main or the other agent. A file outside any Git repository is a separate case, not automatically a forbidden main-checkout write.

Apply the scenario to the exact operation, code paths and acceptance criteria in the retained description. Record the input, actual result, expected result, source revision and a durable artifact. A failure must be tied to this outcome before reopening; a passing unrelated suite must not close it.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## What
CORRECTED DESIGN (superseding the original "broadly allow EnterWorktree" framing, Alex 2026-09-08):
EnterWorktree's own tool description says it "Creates an isolated worktree (via git or configured
hooks) and switches the session into it" -- it can itself create a worktree at a model-supplied
path, not merely switch into a pre-existing one. Broadly trusting EnterWorktree via a static
permissions.allow entry would therefore open the exact same location-bypass hole (a worktree
landing outside <repo>/.worktrees/, GH-329's failure mode) that agent-tools PR#610
(block-raw-worktree-add, agent a3105ae878f4afee3) closes for the git-argv-level case
(git worktree add/remove/move). A blanket EnterWorktree permission grant would let a caller route
around that same guard through a different tool.

The fix must be PATH-SCOPED, not broad:
- A target under the canonical, rig-sanctioned <repo>/.worktrees/<name> -> auto-allow, no
  interactive prompt (this is the actual friction rig-cli#418 exists to remove).
- A target anywhere else -> stays gated (prompt, or deny/hatch-escalate, mirroring
  block-raw-worktree-add's policy for the git-level case).

Because a static permissions.allow / permissions.deny entry cannot express a path-conditional
decision, the mechanism is a PreToolUse agent-hook (PR#298 already registered the EnterWorktree
matcher into the CC hook bridge specifically so a hook like this can fire), which returns
hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision:"allow" for the canonical-path case to suppress the
interactive prompt, and falls through to normal gating otherwise. This hook must REUSE, not
reimplement, the canonical-.worktrees/-path-check primitives already built in agent-tools
PR#610 (repo_root / _target_is_sanctioned / _worktrees_dir_escapes_repo in
block-raw-worktree-add/block_raw_worktree_add.py) -- coordinate with agent a3105ae878f4afee3
before building a second implementation of the same policy.

rig-cli's own job narrows accordingly: this ticket is no longer about adding a permission-allow
entry in riglib/permissions.py. It is about ensuring rig correctly PROVISIONS/REGISTERS whatever
new agent-hook ends up implementing the EnterWorktree path check (via the existing agent_hooks
catalog plumbing, riglib/catalog.py), and that rig status/drift correctly reports when that hook
is missing from a repo's installed agent-hooks -- the same way rig already reports drift for
every other catalog-sourced agent-hook. The hook implementation itself likely belongs in
agent-tools (possibly a new hook, or an extension of block-raw-worktree-add's shared policy
functions), not in rig-cli.

## Why (motivation)
Alex, 2026-09-07/08: hit this live mid-session (a subagent blocked on the EnterWorktree permission prompt) and reacted with real frustration -- this is exactly the kind of worktree-location friction he told me to eliminate structurally, not patch around per-session.

## User impact
Every agent working in this ecosystem across every repo hits an unnecessary interactive approval prompt the first time it enters a worktree the sanctioned way, breaking autonomous/background sessions that have nobody watching to answer the prompt, and forcing whoever IS watching to interrupt what they're doing to click through it.

## Cost of inaction
Autonomous and background sessions silently stall at this exact prompt with no one to answer it, and every interactive session keeps eating an avoidable interruption -- the friction Alex already flagged keeps recurring machine to machine, repo to repo, because the one-off manual patch from today doesn't propagate anywhere.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Rig's baseline permission provisioning learns EnterWorktree as a known permission key and provisions a sensible default allow rule during rig apply for every configured harness kind that supports it, mirroring how other baseline tool permissions are already provisioned
- [ ] The provisioned rule is scoped sensibly -- broadly trusting EnterWorktree is reasonable given the actual cross-agent-worktree-entry security concern is already handled by the enterworktree-foreign-guard agent-hook (a separate layer), but document that reasoning inline in the permission entry per this repo's own house rule that every permission/agent-hook toggle needs an inline comment explaining what it is for and what it does NOT weaken
- [ ] rig status reports drift if a repo's settings file is missing this baseline entry, same as it does for other rig-managed permission baselines
- [ ] Regression test: a fresh rig apply on a clean config provisions the EnterWorktree allow rule; rig status on a config missing it reports drift; re-apply is idempotent
- [ ] - [ ] The EnterWorktree path-check mechanism is PATH-SCOPED (auto-allow only for a target
      resolving under <repo>/.worktrees/<name>; anything else stays gated/denied), not a broad
      EnterWorktree permission grant.
- [ ] The path-check logic is NOT duplicated: it reuses (verified against, or literally
      shares/SYNCs with) the canonical-path primitives already built in agent-tools PR#610
      (block-raw-worktree-add's repo_root / _target_is_sanctioned / _worktrees_dir_escapes_repo),
      confirmed by direct coordination with agent a3105ae878f4afee3 rather than independently
      re-derived.
- [ ] Whatever agent-hook ends up implementing the EnterWorktree PreToolUse path decision is
      correctly provisioned by rig during `rig apply` via the existing agent_hooks catalog
      plumbing (riglib/catalog.py), keyed off harness.kind exactly like every other agent-hook.
- [ ] `rig status` reports drift if a repo's installed agent-hooks are missing this hook, same as
      it does for every other catalog-sourced agent-hook descriptor.
- [ ] Regression test: a fresh `rig apply` on a clean config provisions the hook descriptor;
      `rig status` on a config missing it reports drift; re-apply is idempotent.
- [ ] Live confirmation: an EnterWorktree call into the canonical <repo>/.worktrees/<name>
      location no longer triggers an interactive approval prompt, while a call targeting a path
      outside .worktrees/ still gets gated.

Alex 5 Sep asked whether anti-slop statistics are collected. The apply-time preview is the intended collector and currently never emits counts on a repo that also carries the canonical oxc config.

A person running rig apply to turn on Oxlint never sees the before/after error and warning delta. They have to know to run oxlint JSON by hand, so the promised apply-time statistics stay at skipped forever.

## Cost of inaction
Every future first-time anti-slop apply will report skipped preview. The 5 Sep statistics question stays unanswered at the apply boundary.

## What
omp's web_search tool falls through providers. Perplexity is a default provider (anonymous cookie fallback to https://www.perplexity.ai/). Without a Perplexity account that path returns a Sign-up wall instead of search results. omp exposes providers.webSearchExclude ('Providers that web_search should never use, even as fallbacks'); a prior session set `omp config webSearchExclude perplexity`, which wrote providers.webSearchExclude: [perplexity] into ~/.omp/agent/config.yml. A one-off `omp config` write is session/machine state that `rig apply` will not restore. Search is a load-bearing agent tool; it must stay working across omp upgrades, config.yml resets, and new machines the same way tools.approvalMode already does.

## User impact
When an agent needs live web facts (docs, current events, APIs), web_search currently depends on a hand-edit in ~/.omp/agent/config.yml. ## Cost of inaction
Every new machine and every omp config reset silently regresses search to the signup wall. Agents keep hitting Perplexity, wasting a fallback slot, and returning unusable 'Sign up' text. The workaround (`omp config set providers.webSearchExclude perplexity`) stays tribal knowledge instead of a reconcilable rig setting.

Classification (kind), data-driven in `riglib/stats/hatches.py`:

Data model: new `HatchEvent` / `HatchAggregate` in `riglib/stats/hatches.py`. Do NOT cram into ToolInvocation/Aggregate. dedup by (ts, hook) preferring overrides

## What
riglib/stats/taxonomy.py defines OUR_CLIS = frozenset({"rig", "tg", "draw", "3d", "task", "dev", "pm", "research"}) - the list of ecosystem CLI program names 'rig stats show' recognizes as ours when detected inside a shell command string. This list is missing three real installed ecosystem CLI binaries: harness (harness-cli, local checkout at /Users/ultra/xp/harness-cli/bin/harness), qa (qa-cli, local checkout at /Users/ultra/xp/qa-cli/bin/qa), and stt (stt-cli, local checkout at /Users/ultra/xp/stt-cli/bin/stt). Any invocation of these three tools is currently miscategorized as 'other' instead of 'ours' in the adoption report, silently undercounting real ecosystem-tool usage. Separately (and out of scope for the narrow fix tracked here — larger feature), there is no subcommand-level breakdown anywhere in riglib/stats/: categorize() in taxonomy.py maps a shell invocation to CLI-name only, never CLI-name+subcommand, so 'rig stats show' cannot answer 'how much is task new vs task list vs task classify used', only 'how much task-cli in general is used'. Not a duplicate of rig-cli#316, which is about delegated-agent transcript log-parsing depth, a different bug.

## Why (motivation)
rig stats show's adoption report is the CTO-facing signal for ecosystem-tool adoption across harnesses. Three real, installed CLIs (harness, qa, stt) are silently excluded from the 'ours' bucket, understating real adoption. Separately, the report has no per-subcommand granularity, so it can't answer usage questions at the level teams actually care about (e.g. task new vs task list).

## User impact
Anyone reading rig stats show's adoption numbers gets an artificially low ecosystem-CLI adoption ratio (harness/qa/stt calls fall into 'other'), and cannot break down usage of any single CLI by subcommand to see which features are actually used.

## Cost of inaction
The adoption metric keeps silently undercounting three real ecosystem CLIs indefinitely, and any decision made from rig stats show (e.g. justifying investment in a specific tool or subcommand) is made on data that both undercounts totals and can never show sub-command-level usage.

## What

This is a distinct gap from the bash-level osascript rule (a sibling change): that rule only ever sees bash tool argv, so it cannot see a command shelled out to from inside eval code.

Fix: riglib/permissions.py -- GuardRule gains a scope field (default ("bash",)) and a new "code_pattern" matcher, validated by __post_init__ (code_pattern rules must scope to ("eval",) and take exactly one token, the needle; every other rule stays pinned to ("bash",)). New deny rule eval-osascript-spawn catches osascript spawned from eval code. riglib/omp_guard.py -- _rules_ts() emits the new scope field; the generated TS gains a matchesCodePattern() helper (quoted-string needle match, so execSync("osascript ...") / Bun.spawn(["osascript", ...]) match but a bare mention in a // comment does not) and the tool_call handler now branches on event.toolName === "eval" to scan the cell's source text against code_pattern rules before the bash-only fast path -- bash-argv rules explicitly skip code_pattern rules and vice versa. tests/test_omp_guard.py -- registry coverage assertions extended; the OMP-only-extras set now includes eval-osascript-spawn (no claude-code or opencode counterpart is possible, those harnesses have no eval-tool-code inspection mechanism); six new bun fixture cases cover deny-via-execSync, deny-via-Bun.spawn, the sanctioned computer helper path staying allowed, a bare comment mention staying allowed, a missing code field staying allowed, and the ask-confirm-no path.

## Why (motivation)
The eval tool's cell code runs with full Bun/Node + tool-bridge access and is explicitly documented as not sandboxed. Every other raw-command surface (bash argv) already has an osascript deny rule, but that rule is blind to code executed inside an eval cell, so an agent blocked by a TCC-protected bash/read path can trivially route around the guard by shelling out to osascript from eval code -- reproducing the exact unapprovable Automation prompt loop the bash-level rule exists to prevent.

Anyone running agents through this harness (e.g. rig-managed Claude Code or omp sessions) is protected from a specific repeated-permission-prompt annoyance and a real sandbox hole: today, if an agent needs a TCC-protected file (like a folder under Downloads) and its normal file/bash tools are denied by macOS privacy protections, it can silently fall back to running raw AppleScript/osascript from inside an eval code cell to drive apps like Finder directly -- popping the same macOS "Automation" permission dialog the user has already been repeatedly declining, and doing so through a code path the existing guard never inspected. After this fix, that fallback is blocked by the same guard rule system as the bash-level equivalent, so the user stops seeing that unapprovable prompt loop and the sandbox boundary holds for the eval tool too.

## Cost of inaction
The eval-cell osascript path stays a live sandbox bypass: any agent whose bash/read tools hit a TCC-protected path (as already observed in production, see the cited session log) can keep routing around denial by shelling out to osascript from eval code, regenerating the same unapprovable macOS Automation/TCC permission-prompt loop the user has already had to repeatedly deny, with no guard coverage until this is merged.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## What
[PR #487](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/pull/487) (merged as d933f56, generalizing cc-restore's exact-session tmux resume to omp and Codex CLI) has several correctness/design bugs surfaced by independent multi-model AI review (Sonnet/quality, Fable/architect, Opus/correctness) run against its diff on 2026-09-10 to satisfy the gh ship review-quorum gate for [#494](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/494). None are merge artifacts from the #487/#484/#485 sibling-feature merge -- they are pre-existing in the feature as authored. (1) render_codex_restore's 'codex resume --last' fallback resumes the globally most-recent codex session, not the most-recent session IN THAT CWD like the claude/omp fallbacks, so two panes with stale rollout files can both resume the same wrong session. (2) newest_session_for_cwd (codex-save) scans local-date directories oldest-day-first then ls -t within a day, so a session started yesterday but still live (recent mtime) can lose to a dead session from today scanned first for the same cwd -- claude-save and omp-save use pure mtime ordering and don't have this bug. (3) LOOKBACK_DAYS=2 with its seq range actually scans 3 calendar days, contradicting the docstring, inline comment, and docs which all say 2. (4) managed_scripts() only includes the omp/codex save/restore scripts and map file when that harness's restore-enabled flag is true (unlike cc_restore's always-on pair), so disabling a knob after a prior apply leaves stale scripts on disk invisible to rig status's drift report forever, violating this repo's own 'drift is surfaced both ways, never silently reconciled' rule. (5) encode_cwd (omp-save) falls back to encoding the full absolute path for cwds outside /Users/ultra the same way as in-HOME paths, so two different absolute paths can alias to the same slug and silently record the wrong project's session. (6) The three restore scripts run sequentially in one chained resurrect hook; since each save script's process-tree walk can match a pane running multiple harnesses (e.g. an omp session that spawned claude as a subprocess), a second restore command can get typed into a pane the first restore command already claimed, before the pane's current command reflects the exec.

## Why (motivation)
These are real correctness bugs in shipped tmux session-restore logic that runs unattended after every machine reboot; they were caught by AI review specifically run to satisfy a ship gate, not by the PR's own test suite (all new tests are string-presence assertions on rendered script text, none exercise the actual bash logic's runtime behavior), so they would otherwise ship silently and go untracked.

## User impact
A user relying on tmux session-restore across a reboot can silently resume the wrong coding-agent session (or no session, or a double-typed restore command) in a pane, losing continuity of an in-progress task without any error or warning -- and rig status will never flag the underlying drift (orphaned scripts) that results from toggling the feature off.

## Cost of inaction
The bugs remain live in main indefinitely; each additional user who enables the new restore knobs hits them at their next real reboot, and the root causes get harder to distinguish from unrelated tmux/resurrect issues the longer they go unfixed and untracked.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] the codex restore fallback resumes the most-recent codex session scoped to the pane's cwd, matching the claude/omp fallback contract (or the mismatch is documented as an accepted limitation with a reason)
- [ ] the codex session-discovery scan uses pure mtime ordering across all scanned day-directories (not day-first then mtime-within-day), matching the claude/omp save scripts' approach
- [ ] the lookback-days scan range and its docstring, inline comment, and docs page all agree on the actual number of days scanned
- [ ] disabling either new restore knob after a prior apply is either detected as drift by rig status, or the stale scripts are actively removed on the next apply
- [ ] the cwd-to-slug encoding for an out-of-HOME cwd either produces a collision-free encoding or explicitly skips recording that pane instead of guessing
- [ ] a pane matched by more than one harness's process-tree detector cannot receive two chained restore commands (either detection is made mutually exclusive per-pane, or restore verifies the pane's current command settled before the next chained script runs)

## Worked verification example

### Ticket-specific check

**Operation under review:** tmux clipboard command re-resolves PATH and WAYLAND_DISPLAY per invocation, risking apply-vs-status drift on Linux.

**Original problem context (historical statement, not a new observation):** riglib/tmux.py's _detect_platform_clipboard_command() (~lines 221-240) probes shutil.which(...) and os.environ.get("WAYLAND_DISPLAY") to auto-detect the Linux or macOS clipboard command. It is called via _resolve_clipboard_command() (~lines 243-253) from inside build_tmux() (~line 1860). build_tmux() is invoked fresh on every separate CLI process run, so `rig apply` and a later, independent `rig status` each re-probe PATH and environment variables for the clipboard command rather than sharing one cached plan-time resolution -- despite the adjacent comment claiming plan-time determinism ("Resolve tmux ONCE here (plan time) so every render is deterministic across invocations", ~line 1849, referring to tmux_bin). The clipboard command resolution is genuinely re-computed per process; it is never persisted or reused between the apply and status invocations. Found during review of already-merged PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/pull/484 (fix(tmux): copy-mode clipboard bindings), not yet fixed.

**Expected outcomes from this ticket, not invented from its title:**
- The resolved clipboard command is persisted as part of the stored or serialized plan (or otherwise memoized for the process or session) so `rig apply` and a subsequent `rig status` compare against the SAME resolved clipboard command instead of each independently re-probing PATH or WAYLAND_DISPLAY.
- A regression test simulates a PATH or WAYLAND_DISPLAY change occurring between an apply call and a status call and proves no spurious drift is reported, given the user's actual tmux config did not change.

**Illustrative scenario for this concern (not an observed reproduction):** Only one paid model is available. It performs four separate reviews with security, performance, correctness and test-design prompts. Four roles are covered, but the report still states one underlying model; it does not invent four independent models or disable the role requirement.

Apply the scenario to the exact operation, code paths and acceptance criteria in the retained description. Record the input, actual result, expected result, source revision and a durable artifact. A failure must be tied to this outcome before reopening; a passing unrelated suite must not close it.

## Original technical scope, acceptance and delivery history

## What
riglib/tmux.py's _detect_platform_clipboard_command() (~lines 221-240) probes shutil.which(...) and os.environ.get("WAYLAND_DISPLAY") to auto-detect the Linux or macOS clipboard command. It is called via _resolve_clipboard_command() (~lines 243-253) from inside build_tmux() (~line 1860). build_tmux() is invoked fresh on every separate CLI process run, so `rig apply` and a later, independent `rig status` each re-probe PATH and environment variables for the clipboard command rather than sharing one cached plan-time resolution -- despite the adjacent comment claiming plan-time determinism ("Resolve tmux ONCE here (plan time) so every render is deterministic across invocations", ~line 1849, referring to tmux_bin). The clipboard command resolution is genuinely re-computed per process; it is never persisted or reused between the apply and status invocations. Found during review of already-merged PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/pull/484 (fix(tmux): copy-mode clipboard bindings), not yet fixed.

## Why (motivation)
Real latent bug surfaced via code review of merged PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/pull/484's clipboard auto-detection logic in riglib/tmux.py (_detect_platform_clipboard_command, _resolve_clipboard_command, and build_tmux); not caught before merge and not yet fixed.

## User impact
Linux users can see `rig status` report false config drift (or apply-vs-status flapping) purely because PATH or WAYLAND_DISPLAY differs subtly between invocation contexts (e.g. an interactive shell versus a cron, systemd, or other non-interactive context), even though nothing about their actual tmux config changed.

## Cost of inaction
The bug keeps confusing Linux users about whether their tmux config actually applied cleanly, and erodes trust in rig status's drift detection more broadly.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The resolved clipboard command is persisted as part of the stored or serialized plan (or otherwise memoized for the process or session) so `rig apply` and a subsequent `rig status` compare against the SAME resolved clipboard command instead of each independently re-probing PATH or WAYLAND_DISPLAY.
- [ ] A regression test simulates a PATH or WAYLAND_DISPLAY change occurring between an apply call and a status call and proves no spurious drift is reported, given the user's actual tmux config did not change.

The cache file grows forever on any machine with session-log rotation/cleanup, silently degrading rig stats performance again over a long enough timeline -- the same class of problem just fixed, just on a longer time horizon.

Every issue in the twelve-repository ecosystem receives an explicit, source-grounded disposition, ownership, requirements provenance and verification status. ## Scope
rig-cli, agent-tools, harness-cli, review-cli, task-cli, tg-cli, qa-cli, draw-cli, stt-cli, research-cli, dev-cli and pm-cli. All issue states and all available history, with an additional last-ten-days lens; not merely the 715 rows in the uploaded screenshot sweep.

title: Spec review publication access: verify GitHub or @glide.vc authentication without a fake client-side gate
body:
## Source request — editorial quotation
> Все спеки сделай доступными для ревью на spec-dev или подними альтернативный сайт. Если возможно, хорошо бы добавить авторизацию через GitHub или адреса @glide.vc. Такой вход я добавлял в e2e-портале hyperide/hyper-ext-e2e.

Source: Alex's explicit request in this conversation, 2026-09-10; spelling and punctuation corrected, scope unchanged.

## Current factual boundary
The alternative review reader is public. Opening GitHub to submit a review uses GitHub's authentication; it does NOT restrict who can read the static site. The connected GitHub reads for `hyperide/hyper-ext-e2e` returned 404. That does not establish that the repository is absent; its code and auth implementation have not been inspected with the currently available authorization. No token or OAuth secret has been copied into the public site.

Parent: https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/521
Specification: https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/blob/docs/full-grooming-2026-09-10/docs/specs/recovery/01-retrospective-v4.md
V4 publication evidence: https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/tree/docs/full-grooming-2026-09-10/docs/grooming/v4-2026-09-10

## Acceptance
- [ ] Authorized read of the existing e2e portal identifies the actual provider, server-side session validation and organization/domain policy. Reuse it only after verifying the implementation, not its name.
- [ ] A deployment target with server-side execution and authorized OAuth/email configuration is available. An input box, localStorage flag or static login button is not access control.
- [ ] GitHub access is checked against the explicitly agreed account/team policy; arbitrary successful GitHub login is not automatically authorization.
- [ ] Email admission verifies ownership of the exact `glide.vc` domain using a server-validated claim, not an unverified user-entered address or a suffix such as `glide.vc.attacker.example`.
- [ ] Negative tests cover unauthenticated reads, denied identities, expired sessions, callback state/PKCE, login CSRF, logout and direct static/API access to protected content.
- [ ] Public reading remains clearly labeled until the protected deployment is actually verified. Do not break the working public review URL or claim private access from a design-only implementation.

## Example
A reviewer opens a deep link to a retrospective section in a private browser session. In a protected deployment the server redirects to the real login flow and then returns to that exact section only for an authorized identity. Accessing the underlying Markdown/API directly must enforce the same policy.

This is an optional access-control follow-up, not a blocker for the user-authorized public alternative, and not permission to weaken or bypass an existing authorization boundary.
